World.title: Missing New York grandmother found dead near Las Vegas airport after mysterious Bitcoin texts
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

A New York grandmother who vanished without a trace while visiting Las Vegas earlier this month has been found dead, her family announced Friday.

Alisa Goods, a 63-year-old grandmother of five, was reported missing Aug. 10, two days after she was last seen leaving a friend's apartment near Maryland Parkway and Tropicana Avenue, according to her family and a missing person report obtained by KLAS-TV.

Las Vegas Metropolitan Police responded early Thursday after a caller reported a "deceased woman in a drainage ditch area near Wayne Newton Boulevard and the Terminal 1 parking garage at Harry Reid International Airport," according to KTNV.

NEW YORK GRANDMOTHER VANISHES IN LAS VEGAS AS FAMILY GETS MYSTERIOUS TEXTS FROM HER PHONE ASKING FOR BITCOIN

Officers located a woman who was later identified as Goods and pronounced dead, the outlet reported.

"Our hearts are broken. We were notified that my aunt was found—unfortunately, not the way we wanted her to be," Goods' niece, Alana Calloway, said in a statement provided to the station.

FAMILY CHECKS LAS VEGAS MORGUES IN DESPERATE SEARCH FOR MISSING NEW YORK GRANDMOTHER

"This is an unimaginable time," the statement continued. "Words cannot describe the pain our family is experiencing right now. We just want to thank the public for the outpouring of love, support, and prayers. We also want to thank the media for helping bring attention to this situation. This hurts so deeply. We are still trying to learn the details surrounding her death. We ask for continued prayers and privacy as we grieve."

Police reviewed surveillance footage that appeared to show Goods "falling down an embankment, getting back up and then collapsing" on Aug. 8, the day she disappeared, with "no further movement observed after that," according to KTNV.

SEARCH UNDERWAY FOR AUSTRALIAN WOMAN WHO VANISHED AFTER SENDING MESSAGE ABOUT GOING FOR A HIKE NEAR LAS VEGAS

Additional surveillance video from that day showed a woman believed to be Goods near the airport that afternoon, the station reported.

Fox News Digital has reached out to the Las Vegas Metropolitan Police Department for additional information.

Goods had been staying with her longtime friend Roger John, who told KLAS-TV that she left his apartment around 12:45 p.m. Aug. 8 to take a bus to a nearby CVS to buy iron pills but never returned.

"Last I saw her, she was going down the stairs. And I said, 'OK, see you later,' And that's the last time I saw her," John told the station.

John said he was not immediately alarmed because Goods sometimes spent hours shopping. When she failed to return, however, he began calling and texting her before contacting her family.

"This is not like her to just go missing," Calloway previously told the outlet. "She has a family that loves her, cares about her. We want her home and want her home safe and alive."

SCAMMERS EXPLOIT NANCY GUTHRIE CASE WITH QR CODE MONEY REQUESTS, PIMA COUNTY SHERIFF WARNS

The mystery surrounding Goods' disappearance deepened when her family said they began receiving unusual text messages from her phone on Aug. 12, four days after she was last seen.

The sender allegedly asked for gas money and Bitcoin , requests that raised suspicions because Goods did not drive and did not have a car in Las Vegas, according to her family.

"I said, 'What do you need gas for? The car?' My aunt does not drive. There is no car," Calloway told CBS News.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

The family previously said the messages raised concerns that Goods may have been kidnapped. It was not immediately clear Friday who sent the messages.

Fox News Digital's Stephen Sorace contributed to this report.

World.title: Canadian prime minister suspends trade talks with U.S., setting new 50% tariffs in motion
World.content:
Trade talks with Canada collapsed late Friday night, setting in motion steep 50% tariffs on a wide swath of Canadian goods. The duties went into effect at the stroke of midnight.

After weeks of talks, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney announced that while important progress had been made, “that progress has not been enough to meet our objectives for Canadians.”

“As a result, this evening, I have decided to suspend trade negotiations with the U.S. and have directed Canada’s negotiators to return to Ottawa,” Carney said in an emailed statement minutes before the deadline.

The tariffs impact about $20 billion worth of U.S. imports from Canada, according to the U.S. Trade Representative’s office. The import taxes will hit everything from hockey sticks, to some building materials, liquors and certain kinds of clothing.

Carney says Canada will immediately retaliate against the U.S. “Canada will match those tariffs dollar for dollar to protect our workers and businesses,” he said.

The failure by American and Canadian trade negotiators to reach a deal came after nearly two weeks of furious talks. It was also a dramatic reversal from Tuesday, when Trump paused the tariffs for three days, writing on social media that the two sides “have a DEAL!”

Officials on both sides had seemed optimistic about a deal up until the very last moment. On Thursday, the Canadian minister responsible for U.S. trade relations met with U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer for several hours.

“We’re very close, we continue to make progress and we’re going to stay here and do the work that is necessary until we get to that point,” Dominic LeBlanc told reporters as he left Greer’s office late Thursday.

Canadian negotiators met again with their U.S. counterparts on Friday and talks stretched until the final hours of the day. Officials remained at the U.S. Trade Representative’s office past 10:30pm E.T. Friday. But ultimately, the two sides were unable to reach a compromise.

In his statement, Carney said “last-minute changes in the U.S. proposed terms were unfair, uneconomic, and called into question the reliability of any deal.”

“We have recognised from the beginning that America has changed, and that we will not return to our old relationship,” Carney said. “Canada has what the world wants. And we will not allow any nation to determine our future.”

Greer said in a statement early Saturday that Canada “declined to finalize the trade deal under the terms agreed earlier this week.”

“Despite the U.S. offer to Canada to receive the best treatment of any major exporter to our market, new demands and walk backs of other commitments by Canada have upended the careful balance reached in the past days,” he said.

Greer said that a point of contention was Canada continuing to maintain its retaliation against the United States “including, among other things, flat-out prohibitions on certain American goods and services.” Those bans, introduced by Canada’s provinces on the sale of American alcohol, were introduced in 2025 in retaliation for earlier waves of Trump’s tariffs on Canada.

As talks wore on this week, the government of Carney faced some pushback from premiers of Canada’s provinces back home.

Manitoba premier Wab Kinew said the Canadian federal government should “fight” Trump.

A particular sticking point was a request from Carney to the provincial premiers to lift their bans on American alcohol sales.

Quebec premier Christine Fréchette said Thursday that she was still “analyzing” the request, CBC reported. Other premiers, such as Ontario’s Doug Ford — who leads the country’s most populous region — did not make any public remarks on Thursday or earlier Friday.

However, Ford wrote on X after Carney’s announcement, “The prime minister has my full support for a strong response—tariff for tariff, dollar for dollar.” Ford said Canada “needs to stand together more united than ever before.”

The prime minister had previously said Trump’s threatened tariffs would amount to a “direct violation” of the United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement, which Trump had negotiated and signed during his first term.

The U.S. Chamber of Commerce warned in a statement this week that “higher tariffs would damage both economies, drive up costs for U.S. families, further disrupt critical supply chains, and risk the 13 million American jobs that depend on” the North American trade pact.

After Carney’s announcement on Friday, the Canadian Chamber of Commerce, seemed to agree, calling it “a body blow to North American competitiveness in this self-defeating trade saga.”

“Americans will see their costs go up, and Canadians will see customers, investment and small businesses disappear,” said Candace Laing, president & CEO of the Canadian Chamber of Commerce.

The new tariffs were imposed under presidential authority granted by Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930, which has never been deployed before.

The law allows the White House to implement duties of up to 50% on any foreign trade partner that “discriminates” against U.S. commerce.

Nonetheless, the new Canada tariffs are all but certain to be challenged in court.

Canadian officials had been hoping to convince the White House to drop the Section 338 tariffs entirely. In addition to that goal, they had also been looking for a lower tariff rate on industrial products such as steel and aluminum that were imposed under Section 232 of the Trade Act, CBC News and Bloomberg have reported.

On Wednesday, Bloomberg reported that American negotiators had agreed to lower the current tariffs on cars and metals from 25% to 15%.

In his statement early Saturday, Greer said that the U.S. had offered “significant tariff reductions on steel, aluminum, autos, and lumber,” without providing specifics. “This is a missed opportunity for Canada to partner with the United States,” he said.

Spokespeople for Canadian officials involved in the talks have repeatedly declined to provide additional details about the negotiations to NBC News.

But Greer previously said that the new 50% duties on Canada were effectively payback for Ottawa’s retaliation against prior tranches of Trump’s tariffs.

“The policy basis for those duties are related to measures that Canada took against the United States,” Greer said last week. “So I’ve got two countries in the world that have retaliated against the United States for trade measures: the People’s Republic of China and Canada. That’s not the kind of company you really want to be running in.”

Last year, Trump briefly responded to China’s retaliation by raising tariffs into the triple digits. Talks between Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and China’s vice premier over months eventually diffused the tensions and tariffs were lowered.

World.title: Trump tries new midterm message to supporters: ‘Pretend, please, that I’m on the ballot’
World.content:
President Donald Trump wants his supporters to think beyond his endorsed candidates and imagine that he is on the ballot when they vote in this year’s midterm elections.

The president made his new pitch Friday night in South Carolina at a rally in support of Sen. Darline Graham, urging the crowd to back her in Tuesday’s Senate GOP runoff.

“The problem that we have is, they say that Trump does great when he’s on the ballot, but when he’s not on the ballot, his people don’t come and they don’t vote for senators, congressmen, and other Republicans,” Trump said.

“So what I really want you to do is pretend, please, that I’m on the ballot. Just come and vote. It’s so important,” he said.

Trump suggested the MAGA faithful also take that approach in other elections as well, saying, “We have to get Darline and other people elected.”

President Donald Trump speaks during a campaign rally for Sen. Darline Graham at Myrtle Beach Convention Center in Myrtle Beach, S.C., on Friday. Saul Loeb / AFP via Getty Images

The president drove home the point near the end of his remarks about an hour later by telling supporters to think of him when they vote.

“I am on the ballot. We’re all on the ballot. Our country’s on the ballot,” Trump said.

That message to supporters comes as six of Trump’s endorsed candidates failed to earn the Republican nomination in their respective primaries for House or governor this month. Before August, only three Trump-backed candidates lost their bids in those contests so far this year.

The president’s endorsement of Graham for a full six-year term did not secure her a majority of the vote in the initial primary, and some of Trump’s supporters at Friday’s rally told NBC News they still had reservations about her following a poor debate performance on Tuesday.

During his nearly 90 minutes onstage Friday, Trump made no mention of the other person who actually is on the ballot in Tuesday’s runoff: GOP Rep. Ralph Norman.

World.title: Missing New York City grandmother found dead near airport in Las Vegas
World.content:
The body of a missing 63-year-old grandmother from New York City was found near Harry Reid International Airport in Las Vegas, police said Friday.

Police said security camera footage showed that Alisa Goods had fallen down an embankment and collapsed and couldn’t be seen from the adjacent roadway, Wayne Newton Boulevard.

Alisa Goods. Courtesy Alana Calloway

Her body was found in a drainage ditch near a parking structure Thursday after someone called to report a body near the airport, the Las Vegas Metropolitan Police Department said in a statement.

The security video is from Aug. 8, it said, the day Goods’ family said she went missing in Las Vegas while visiting a friend. Goods was from Brooklyn, family has said.

Alana Calloway, Goods’ niece, said her aunt was visiting a friend in Las Vegas and was headed to a pharmacy before she disappeared.

Her family said that after her disappearance, someone using her phone number texted relatives to ask for help in the form of bitcoin or a CashApp transfer.

01:02 Family of woman missing in Las Vegas plead for answers 00:00 00:00

Police believe the texts may have come from scammers using “spoofing” technology to present themselves as texting under Goods’ number. They said they didn’t believe Goods was in danger at the time.

Police said the remains’ identity was preliminary. Cause and manner of death were unavailable.

Calloway said the family is grieving.

“Our hearts are broken,” she said in a statement Friday. “Words cannot describe the pain our family is experiencing right now. We just want to thank the public for the outpouring of love, support, and prayers.”

World.title: Karoline Leavitt to work for Trump-affiliated super PAC after leaving White House
World.content:
Press secretary Karoline Leavitt will work for President Donald Trump’s super PAC MAGA Inc. after she leaves her post at the White House, she said Friday.

Leavitt, 28, told reporters aboard Air Force One that she will return to work for the super PAC, for which she served as a spokesperson before joining Trump’s 2024 campaign, though she did not specify what her new title will be.

MAGA Inc. did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Leavitt’s new role.

Speaking briefly in the press cabin before takeoff, Leavitt told reporters that she will miss the job “but I love my kids even more.” Leavitt added that she and her family will remain in Washington for a while, telling reporters, “You guys will still see me all the time.”

She told reporters that Friday’s flight to South Carolina for a rally supporting Sen. Darline Graham will be her last trip as press secretary, but that she’ll be back on board for the Republican National Committee’s midterm convention scheduled for Sept. 9 and 10.

Leavitt, who became the youngest press secretary in history when she joined the second Trump administration, announced her departure from the White House on Aug. 12.

Trump wrote in a Truth Social post that day that Leavitt was stepping down to “spend more time with her beautiful young children and family.”

The president added that Leavitt “will now be one of my top outside advisors, and an influential voice within the Republican Party, as we work to defy History, and conclusively win the Midterm Elections.”

Leavitt, who gave birth to her second child in May and returned from maternity leave on July 16, wrote in her own post on Aug. 12 that she “felt in my heart that I cannot be the best mom my two young children deserve while devoting the constant time, energy, and attention required of the White House Press Secretary.”

Leavitt worked as an assistant White House press secretary during Trump’s first term before she became the communications director for Rep. Elise Stefanik, R-N.Y.

Leavitt then ran for Congress in New Hampshire, losing to Democratic Rep. Chris Pappas in 2022. She subsequently began working as a spokesperson for MAGA Inc.

After joining Trump’s 2024 campaign, Leavitt gave birth to her first child and returned to work just four days into her maternity leave in the wake of the assassination attempt against Trump at a rally in Butler, Pennsylvania.

As Leavitt leaves her role after 18 months on the job, she will become the second-longest-serving press secretary under Trump after now-Arkansas Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders, who served in the role for almost two years during Trump’s first term.

World.title: Vance’s homecoming is a throwback to 2024 — and a preview for 2026 and 2028: From the Politics Desk
World.content:
Welcome to From the Politics Desk, a daily newsletter that brings you the NBC News Politics team’s latest reporting and analysis from the White House, Capitol Hill and the campaign trail.

In today’s edition, Henry J. Gomez explains what Vice President JD Vance’s Ohio trip says about his midterm role. Plus, Kristen Welker breaks down the stakes for President Donald Trump’ in next week’s South Carolina runoff.

Sign up to receive this newsletter in your inbox every weekday here.

— Adam Wollner

Vance’s homecoming is a throwback to 2024 — and a preview for 2026 and 2028

Analysis by Henry J. Gomez

Vice President JD Vance’s return to his hometown this afternoon was in many ways a preview of the heavy load he will carry for President Donald Trump and the Republican Party on the midterm campaign trail.

Against the backdrop of voters’ mounting affordability concerns, Vance emphasized an uptick in manufacturing jobs during a speech in Middletown, Ohio. He celebrated $1 billion in new investment, including a federal grant, that will help upgrade the Cleveland-Cliffs steel plant where he delivered his remarks. And he urged support for Republican candidates this fall, singling out Sen. Jon Husted, who is running to keep Vance’s old Senate seat, and Vivek Ramaswamy, the party’s nominee for Ohio governor.

“This is not, unfortunately, JFK or FDR‘s Democrat party,” Vance said. “Hell, it’s not even Bill Clinton‘s Democrat Party.”

For the GOP, one notion underpinning the message is that Vance may be uniquely suited to sell it. The factory he visited Friday was the same one — albeit under a different name and ownership — where his late grandfather once toiled as a welder. It’s a detail familiar to those who read Vance’s 2016 memoir, “Hillbilly Elegy,” and one that he has been called on to recount time and again in his young political career to project working-class relatability.

“Papaw was a welder in this place for 40 years, and today his grandson stands here as the vice president of these United States. It’s an amazing thing,” Vance said. “And I’m here with a message from the president of these United States: The future of America, the future of the United States, the future of our homes and communities is going to be built right here in Middletown, Ohio.”

The visit was a throwback to how Vance was used as Trump’s running mate in 2024. His first solo event after joining the ticket that year was in Middletown, at his high school alma mater. Vance then spent the weeks until Election Day largely camped out in other Midwest states, such as Michigan and Wisconsin, and culturally and economically similar parts of Pennsylvania.

As it was then, the idea now is that Vance’s lived experience in a region that people on the coasts dismiss as the Rust Belt helps him connect with blue-collar voters. Energy Secretary Chris Wright, who spoke before Vance today, welcomed the vice president to the stage by declaring him “the leader of the reindustrializing the United States of America.”

Vance, who recently welcomed a fourth child with second lady Usha Vance, has acknowledged that his own political fortunes are tied to this year’s midterm elections. He is the first sitting vice president to serve as the Republican National Committee’s finance chair.

It’s a position that will require him to spend plenty of time raising money — and testing his message — beyond his Midwest comfort zone. And it’s one that could make him a target in a 2028 presidential primary if Republicans suffer big losses.

Uncertain South Carolina race presents key test for Trump

Analysis by Kristen Welker

President Donald Trump is heading to South Carolina tonight to try and boost appointed Sen. Darline Graham ahead of Tuesday’s primary runoff, which will present another test of his sway over Republican voters.

The president encouraged Graham to run to replace her late brother, Sen. Lindsey Graham, on the November ballot. She finished first in the initial primary that featured a crowded field earlier this month, winning 33% of the vote. Graham advanced to a runoff against Rep. Ralph Norman, a staunch conservative and member of the House Freedom Caucus, who won 25% of the primary vote.

The two-week sprint to the runoff has raised new questions about Darline Graham’s candidacy, especially following a flub in a recent debate where she was asked about Taiwan and responded, “I’m not that informed on national security, so, but I do support the military.” She later added, “I’m not a polished politician up here. National security is not my thing, not my area of expertise.”

One GOP strategist told me that there’s disagreement about where Graham currently stands, noting internal polling has shown her both ahead of and trailing Norman. The strategist cautioned not to be surprised if Norman pulls off a win.

The tumultuous South Carolina race comes as Trump’s preferred candidates have suffered some primary losses this month. Along with the South Carolina runoff, the president’s endorsement will also be put to the test on Tuesday in a GOP primary runoff for governor in Oklahoma, where Trump-backed former state Sen. Mike Mazzei is facing off against state Attorney General Gentner Drummond.

But Trump’s visit to South Carolina puts that race front and center heading into next week. Graham also has the backing of other prominent Republicans, including South Carolina Sen. Tim Scott, who chairs the Senate Republicans’ campaign arm.

Scott will be joining “Meet the Press” on Sunday, along with Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., to discuss the latest in the battle for the Senate with the midterms fast approaching.

🗳️ Related: Former South Carolina Gov. Mark Sanford, who ran in the Senate primary, endorsed Norman over Graham. Read more →

World.title: This is what you need (and need to do) to stay safe this hurricane season
World.content:
As a Florida native, I’ve endured a lot of hurricanes and I’ve seen the damage they can cause. If you don’t take proper precautions, the destruction hurricanes leave behind can be catastrophic. This is why it’s important to know how to prepare for a hurricane, and make sure you have all of the supplies necessary to keep you and your family safe. Storms have already started making their way across the United States, with tropical storm Lala impacting Hawaii earlier this week. Plus, a potentially record-breaking El Niño is growing in the Pacific ocean, according to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA).

Power outages, flooding, broken windows and damage to homes and cars from fallen trees are just some of the things you need to be ready for. And while you may have a generator in case the electricity goes out, it’s important that you know how to use it properly to avoid carbon monoxide exposure.

I talked to a meteorologist and professor at the University of Florida to learn what measures you should take to make sure your home withstands a storm, and the best emergency kits and other supplies you should always have handy during hurricane season.

Want more from NBC Selected? 

How to prepare for a hurricane

There are many different ways to prepare your home ahead of a hurricane to prevent damage, and to keep everyone safe, particularly in the event that you lose power during and after the storm.

“If you live by the coast, you should be thinking about storm surge, rainfall, and wind speed,” says Stephen Mullens, a meteorologist and assistant instructional professor of meteorology at the University of Florida’s Department of Geography. “Most fatalities and property damage comes from flooding as a result of both storm surge (water that has been moved from the ocean onto land) and from too much rain during the storm.”

The below preparedness tips are key for dealing with common problems during a hurricane, including flooding, power outages, broken windows from strong winds and fallen trees.

Watch for an evacuation warning: “If you are by the coast, look up whether you are in an evacuation zone,” says Mullens. “If you must evacuate during a storm, you only need to travel just outside the evacuation zone.” State government officials will traditionally issue evacuation warnings at least a few days ahead of a hurricane if not more, depending on what category the storm falls under. Be sure to stay on top of news updates. “You will need to leave before the wind and rain arrives, so your home preparations must happen with a deadline in mind,” says Mullens.

Prepare for flooding: Flooding is not only dangerous and a threat to your safety, but it can also cause irreparable damage to your home, which, even with insurance, can be extremely costly to deal with. Mullens recommends using things like sandbags to blockade your home if possible. “These can help prevent water from seeping under [home] doors and garage doors. Most of the time, you won’t experience the worst-case scenario, and sandbags can really help when flooding is only a few inches,” says Mullens. “No amount of [sandbags] will allow you to stay in an evacuation zone [though]. If flooding is forecast to be more than a foot, then plan to evacuate in case the forecast gets worse or your emergency management deems evacuation to be mandatory.”

Mullens also recommends preparing other areas around your home for excess water, too. “Outside your home, clear your gutters and drainage areas of leaves and other debris,” he says. “You don’t want water backing up and pooling in ways you don’t expect.” If your home does get flooded, there is a very short window of time before it will cause mold growth and become a pain to handle, according to Mullens. “It’s a race against time to prevent the build up of mold in drywall and furniture. If your roof has been damaged, a large tarp will prevent future rain from entering your home,” he says. “Inside, fans and a lot of towels will help dry things out.”

Prepare for strong winds: “To prepare for wind, trim branches on trees and bushes so they won’t hit the house. Bring furniture and outdoor decorations inside,” says Mullens. “For large items, stake and tie them down or they will likely fly away. If you live near the coast, nailing plywood over your windows can prevent damage inside your home from flying debris.” Additionally, make sure your cars aren’t beside trees, especially ones with coconuts or large branches that could fall during the hurricane and damage the body, windows or windshields.

Keep electronics charged: Make sure all your electronics are charged before the storm arrives and be sure to stock up on batteries as needed for things like flashlights and other essential devices. “Charge phones while power remains,” says Mullens. “Write down important information in case your phone’s battery runs out before power is restored.” Depending on the severity of the storm, a power outage is very likely, even if it’s just temporary.

Gas generators are one of the most common appliances that people use to restore power in their homes during and after hurricanes, according to Mullens. If you don’t have or plan on using a generator, there are alternatives you can consider, too. Some batteries work for home appliances, not just small handheld electronic devices, according to Mullens. “Today, large batteries can power an air conditioner, well pump, refrigerator, oven, or microwave for several hours,” says Mullens. “It’s important to assess what you most want to have power during an extended power outage, your ability to store the unit when you don’t need it, and cost to guide your purchases.”

Prepare for a disruption in water supply: A loss in access to clean water is also a common issue during and after a hurricane, so it’s important to make sure you have a plan in case you don’t have water for a few days. “Buy large water jugs for drinking and sanitation. Fill them with water prior to a storm,” says Mullens. “You can also fill a bath tub with water so you can flush your toilets. Most storms won’t be the worst-case scenario, but if it does happen you will want enough water for drinking and food for seven days.”

Buy non-perishable foods: Since losing power is common during and after hurricanes, you won’t have access to traditional kitchen appliances like a refrigerator to keep food fresh, an electric stovetop and oven or microwave, unless you find batteries or power stations suitable for powering them. Be sure to buy shelf-stable foods that don’t require cooking or refrigeration after opening, including canned vegetables and soup, cereal, granola bars, chips and crackers. “All these items can be stored at room temperature for a year unless otherwise noted,” says Mullens. “In the summer, before hurricane season, purchase one to two of these items each shopping trip instead of right before a storm.”

Your hurricane supply list

All of the products below are either recommendations from our experts, NBC Selected staff and/or highly-rated on Amazon and other retailers.

The Jackery Explorer is a large portable power station, similar to a portable power bank you’d use to charge your phone, except it has the ability to juice up home appliances like electric grills and portable air conditioners — though you can also use it to charge a phone. In addition to multiple USB-C ports and a USB-A port, it has three AC wall outlets (the same type you’d use to charge the power station itself), which are suitable for charging kitchen appliances like air fryers and mini fridges for example.

It’s available in versions with higher wattages and ones that come with solar panels to charge the power station. It also has a companion app that allows you to track how much battery it has left and adjust settings like the energy saving mode from your phone.

Brio 5-Gallon Plastic Water Container $ 41.03 Amazon What to know What we like BPA-free

Has a handle

Made of strong plastic Something to note Lids sold separately

To make it easier to store several gallons of fresh water ahead of a hurricane, get 5-gallon jugs like this, which is made of strong BPA-free, polycarbonate plastic. It has a handle on the side for carrying and lifting. Note that it doesn’t come with a lid, so be sure to buy caps along with the jugs.

You can get these 50-pound capacity sandbags in sets of 10 or more. They’re made from strong polypropylene material to protect your home against flooding when placed around the area properly. Each bag comes with a tie to keep the sand inside and is 14 by 26 inches, so it’s tall enough to block a few inches of water. When you’re not using them for hurricane preparedness, the bags can help weigh down tents, trucks, trailers, and awnings, according to the brand.

Shoppers say that the ties on the sandbags do a great job of keeping them closed and that they last at least a few years. Just keep in mind that the bags are not pre-filled, so you will need to purchase sand for them.

This set of batteries from Energizer comes with 24 AA batteries and 24 AAA batteries, all which have a shelf life of up to 10 years, according to the brand. The leak-resistant batteries are suitable for small handheld devices like flashlights, remotes, toys and more. These are also the typical sizes for devices like smoke and carbon monoxide detectors, which are useful, particularly if you plan on using a gas generator when the power goes out.

Thriaid 330-Piece First Aid Kit $ 45.99 Amazon What to know What we like Has handles for carrying

Waterproof

Comes with a handbook Something to note Has a soft-shell design

While a first aid kit is something everyone should have in their home for any and all situations, you should definitely have one ahead of a hurricane. This kit has more than 300 pieces, including several sets of adhesive bandages in multiple sizes and shapes, wound closure strips, gloves, an emergency blanket, a pill box, gauze, wipes and a thermometer.

The kit comes in a rectangular, waterproof bag with a zipper closure and handles for easy carrying. It’s small and weighs less than 2 pounds, so it fits in some glove compartments and backpacks. Its compact size and take-anywhere design is a standout for people who bought it.

In addition to flashlights, you should consider getting a set of bright lanterns to help keep your home illuminated if you lose power during a hurricane. These water-resistant lanterns have strong, 154-lumen LED lights and stand up on their own. They also have handles for carrying that are also suitable for attaching to a belt loop or a loop on a backpack in case you need your hands for something else (they’re also great for camping trips).

The lights come with a set of 12 AA alkaline batteries and each lantern requires three batteries. You can also adjust the brightness of each lantern just by lowering the top of it.

Midland Emergency Crank Weather AM/FM Radio $ 79.99 Amazon What to know What we like Comes with batteries

Has a siren

Has a flashlight Something to note Small

In addition to making sure your phone is charged, you’ll want to have some sort of communication device that you can use during a hurricane, like this crank radio from Midland. The device is around the size of a modern portable speaker, but you can use it to communicate with emergency responders by turning the crank on the side. It’s connected to emergency radio channels so you can stay aware of weather updates, including from the NOAA, according to the brand.

It has a flashlight and tactile (not digital) buttons that adjust the volume and change the channel. Plus, it has an antenna and an automatic siren that turns on to let you know when severe weather is coming, according to the brand.

Frequently asked questions How do you stay safe during a hurricane? It’s extremely important to not wait until the last minute to buy emergency hurricane supplies, since options will be very limited. Be sure to prepare for the most common problems, like flooding, lack of access to fresh water (including for your toilet), fallen trees and branches and power outages, says Mullens. You can do this by buying things like non-perishable foods, bottled water or gallons of water, medication, power stations and making sure your electronics (including your phone) are fully charged. What should you stock up on before a hurricane? Since hurricanes often lead to power outages, you should stock up on things that being without power would affect, Mullens. This includes getting multi-gallon water jugs from stores like Home Depot, Lowe’s or Amazon so you can keep a large supply of water. You should also buy non-perishable foods that don’t have to be refrigerated, including canned foods and dry pantry items. Lastly, you should also stock up on energy by charging all of your portable devices, including a portable power station, and have enough batteries for emergency devices like flashlights. Do you have to worry about hurricanes if you don’t live on a coast? Yes. While hurricanes are definitely a threat to coastlines, areas far from coasts aren’t exempt from experiencing their effects. Additionally, trailers and mobile homes are particularly vulnerable to damage from hurricanes, according to Mullens. "Trailers and mobile homes are lighter and more likely to be damaged than homes built on a foundation. Thinner walls mean debris thrown in the wind are more likely to damage walls and windows,” says Mullens. “Being lighter means wind and flood water is more likely to lift the home off its supports. There may be less to do inside and outside to prepare the home itself, but you will likely need to evacuate earlier than recommended.” How do you use a generator safely during a hurricane? While generators are a great appliance when it comes to providing a lot of power during a hurricane, they also can be dangerous when used improperly because they can expose you to carbon monoxide, according to Mullens. "If you are using a gas-powered generator, the unit must be placed outside with cords running from the generator into the house. It is very common for people to operate generators indoors or in a garage, resulting in the resident dying due to a build-up of carbon monoxide,” he says. “If you are using a large battery, you may want to incorporate solar panels or another method to recharge it in case of an extended outage.”

At NBC Selected, we work with experts who have specialized knowledge and authority based on relevant training and/or experience. We also take steps to ensure all expert advice and recommendations are made independently and without undisclosed financial conflicts of interest.

Stephen Mullens is an assistant instructional professor of meteorology at the University of Florida’s Department of Geography.

World.title: Russian strike on Ukraine kills at least 2, a day after deadly mall attack
World.content:
At least two people were killed in Russian strikes on Ukraine, local authorities said, a day after a deadly attack on a busy shopping center.

Kyiv City Military Administration said one person was killed and several were injured at a warehouse in the capital's Darnytskyi district. The authorities had issued an alert for a ballistic missile earlier in the day.

In the southern city of Zaporizhzhia, a Russian drone killed a man and wounded four people, according to the head of the regional military administration Ivan Fedorov.

The strikes came a day after a series of bombings killed at least 20 people across the country on Friday, including an attack on a Ukrainian shopping mall in the city of Kryvyi Rih which Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy described as "absolutely cynical and despicable," which killed 16.

The president said that after the initial drone strike, a second russian drone hit the center half an hour after the first in what he described as a deliberate attempt to target emergency services.

"Attacks like these are nothing less than terrorist acts," Zelenskyy said.

Rescue operations continued through the night, according to regional military governor Oleksandr Ganzha, who reported nine people missing, including two children.

Rescue services said the attack wounded 130 people, including 23 children.

The United Nations reported that the civilian death toll so far this year had risen to its highest level since the first months of the war.

World.title: U.S. set to impose 50% tariffs on Canada after failed talks; Canada to match them
World.content:
The U.S. was set to impose 50% tariffs on $20 billion worth of Canadian products early Saturday after last-ditch negotiations failed to resolve the latest strain in already tense relations between the historic allies. Canada's leader countered that it would match the tariffs "dollar for dollar."

In a call with reporters late Friday, U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said that Canada had declined to finalize the trade deal under the terms that had been agreed to earlier this week.

In his own statement, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said that the "progress" made in the negotiations was "not been enough to meet our objectives for Canadians."

"As a result, this evening, I have decided to suspend trade negotiations with the U.S. and have directed Canada's negotiators to return to Ottawa," Carney said, adding that "Canada will match those tariffs dollar for dollar to protect our workers and businesses."

Canada sought concessions on Trump tariffs on steel, aluminum, autos and lumber that the United States was unwilling to provide, a senior Trump administration official told reporters. Carney blamed Washington for the breakdown, saying "last-minute changes in the U.S. proposed terms were unfair, uneconomic, and called into question the reliability of any deal." He said he had suspended negotiations and directed Canada's negotiating team to return to Ottawa.

President Trump's import taxes will hit about 5% of what Canada ships to the U.S. every year, including products ranging from hockey sticks to tongue depressors.

But the political impact will likely be even bigger than the economic fallout. Canada has threatened to retaliate against any new tariffs with levies of its own, aggravating a trade fight between countries that sold each other $880 billion worth of goods and services last year.

The tariffs were initially supposed to kick in at 12:01 a.m. Wednesday. But Mr. Trump extended the deadline for three days to allow talks to continue, but the two countries still could not reach an agreement in time.

Earlier this week, Carney had said that "substantial progress has been made, although there is important work still to be done."

The Trump administration currently imposes a 10% tariff on goods from Canada, the U.S.'s second-largest trading partner after Mexico, though most Canadian imports are exempt because they comply with the U.S.-Mexico-Canada Agreement, a trade deal signed during Mr. Trump's first term.

Mr. Trump has had a tense relationship with Canada due to trade, NATO, a dispute over a Detroit-area bridge and his threats to make Canada the U.S.' 51st state.

World.title: Drastic water cuts issued for California, Nevada and Arizona from Colorado River
World.content:
Federal officials announced sharp water cuts for the next two years on Friday for three Western states that rely on the imperiled Colorado River.

Under the Bureau of Reclamation's plan, California, Nevada and Arizona will collectively reduce water use by 1.25 million acre-feet annually during that period, with the possibility of larger cuts depending on conditions.

Arizona will see the biggest cuts, while states upstream — Colorado, Utah, Wyoming and New Mexico — do not face any for now.

Meanwhile, neighboring Mexico will reduce its intake by 250,000 acre-feet under a U.S.-Mexico treaty.

"We've been in this 26-year prolonged drought period," said Andrea Travnicek, the Interior Department's assistant secretary for water and science. "We continue to see a prolonged drought in our future. So continuing to work together as a whole within the basin is going to be extremely important."

The Colorado River serves as a water supply source to an estimated 35 million to 40 million people, according to the Bureau of Reclamation.

The current rules governing the use of the river's water are set to expire in October, and the seven states have been unable to reach a consensus on sharing it over the long term.

Last winter saw the worst snowpack on record for the Colorado River Basin, adding more stress on farmers, industry, wildlife and hydropower producers, as well as tens of millions of people who rely on the waterway, including in dozens of Native American tribes and in two Mexican states.

Years of overuse combined with drought and rising temperatures due to climate change have depleted the country's two largest reservoirs, which are both fed by the Colorado. Lake Mead recently plummeted to its lowest level since it began filling nine decades ago, and Lake Powell did the same about a week later. Their combined storage is the lowest it has been in nearly seven decades.

If the water in Lake Powell falls just 33 more feet, the reservoir will no longer meet the water levels needed to generate hydroelectric power, meaning the water can't move through the dam into the Colorado River.

Negotiators in Arizona thanked California and Nevada for their collaboration on sharing the cuts.

"For 2027 and 2028, the reductions that are now memorialized here will provide substantial stability for folks," said Tom Buschatzke, Arizona Department of Water Resources director. "We'll continue to negotiate and figure out how we're going to operate over a longer-term period, which is what we all want."

JB Hamby, California's chief Colorado River negotiator, said the plan brings "some badly needed near-term certainty at a moment of extraordinary risk," though he called it "a bridge, not a permanent solution."

Officials in Nevada applauded their collaboration with Arizona and California and said a seven-state consensus remains their preferred path for the river.

In Southern Nevada, Kyle Roerink, senior adviser at the conservation group Great Basin Water Network, said efforts to build a new airport and shopping malls and some public land sales have not progressed, reflecting the dire hydrology inked in the federal documents. Further cuts could slow real estate development in metro Las Vegas, he said.

"When the Hoover Dam, a symbol of American fortitude and American power, drops and loses its shine, it can be scary," Roerink said. "But it can also pose itself as a great opportunity for us to prepare for the next hundred years in a meaningful way."

World.title: She was a California comeback story, serving juvenile probation in a UC Davis dorm for killing a teen, when arrested again
World.content:
She was 15 when she was placed on juvenile probation for killing 15-year-old Omari Lowery in Sacramento County. Nearly five years later, she was arrested again — accused of dealing drugs from the UC Davis dorm room where she was serving out the remainder of her sentence, arrest records show.

Officers reported allegedly finding live ammunition hidden in a sock in her dresser, a digital scale, more than 100 plastic baggies, text messages appearing to show drug sales, and $4,121 in cash.

CBS California is not including her name in this article because she was a minor at the time of the original offense. She has not finished her sentence and was still under juvenile commitment when she was arrested as an adult in her UC Davis dorm room.

Records reviewed by CBS California Investigates show she had served roughly three years in secure juvenile custody when a Sacramento County judge found she'd made enough progress to step her down into California's Less Restrictive Programming, or LRP.

The state program lets courts move young offenders out of secure facilities into community-based settings, from halfway houses to, in this case, a university dorm, before their sentence is complete.

She was released into the Underground Scholars program at UC Davis, a state-funded UC program for incarcerated and formerly incarcerated students. She moved into campus housing in December 2025.

She was arrested in her dorm room seven months later.

This is the first story in what CBS California Investigates expects to be an ongoing series on the state's LRP system, as public records requests are fulfilled.

Ammunition allegedly found in a sock drawer

Her probation officer searched her dorm room July 29 and reported allegedly finding marijuana, boxes of vape cartridges, a digital scale, text messages and a price list appearing to show drug sales, cash and ammunition — all items her release conditions barred her from having.

She was charged as an adult in Yolo County with felony possession of ammunition by a prohibited person, misdemeanor possession of ammunition on school grounds, and misdemeanor possession of marijuana for sale, court records show. She was arraigned July 31, pleaded not guilty, and posted a $25,000 bail bond in that case.

That case is separate from the probation violation she now faces in Sacramento County Juvenile Court, tied to her original 2021 case — two proceedings in two counties running in parallel, and her custody status under the juvenile matter is not addressed in the Yolo court record.

Her court order requires weekly meetings with Underground Scholars Director Gunner Johnson as a condition of her placement.

CBS California Investigates has reached out to Johnson with a series of program-related questions.

Featured as a success story

Months before her recent UC Davis arrest, California featured the 20-year-old student as a success story – proof the program works.

Records show she was serving as a youth advocate for the Office of Youth and Community Restoration (OYCR), the state agency that oversees the broader LRP system. A March 2026 OYCR presentation names her in that role.

She's not alone

In 2021, a 17-year-old girl was convicted of murdering Fresno State student Sergio Bonboster. His body was dismembered, burned and dumped in a canal.

The teen, now in her 20s, was reportedly enrolled at Sacramento State last year – released under Project Rebound, the Cal State version of the UC system's Underground Scholars program.

The victim's family publicly protested her early release after serving just two years of her four-year murder sentence.

Sacramento State did not confirm her enrollment, citing privacy.

In Los Angeles, a private company has been running a similar program in student housing on UCLA's sorority row, according to a California Post investigation.

LA County paid the company $1.2 million in 2025 to house nine young adults.

A program with no headcount

Underground Scholars is one of three state-supported pathways moving incarcerated and formerly incarcerated people into California higher education, alongside Cal State's Project Rebound and the Rising Scholars network, the community college system's version of the same program.

Project Rebound enrolled 1,522 students statewide last year across 20 Cal State schools, according to publicly available information. CBS California was unable to find a similar count for the Underground Scholars program on UC campuses. We have requested that information from multiple sources.

CBS California Investigates has filed multiple public records requests for the underlying contracts, funding records, and enrollment data behind this program. This is the first story to publish from that reporting; more will follow as records are received.

What the state won't or can't tell us

California's Office of Youth and Community Restoration, or OYCR, partners with the LRP educational pathway programs — described in an OYCR newsletter as building a 'prison-to-university pipeline.

However, the agency could not tell us how many young people are enrolled in these programs, which schools they're at, and where the state funding goes.

Nor could the state provide recidivism or success rate data related to the total number of participants who violated probation, were arrested or who successfully completed the program.

The agency said that's a county-level responsibility, not the state's, and that collecting it centrally falls outside its authority.

The agency's own public list of Underground Scholars partner campuses does not include UC Davis — the same campus where the young woman at the center of this story was placed. The agency itself featured her as a "youth advocate" in a state presentation earlier this year.

OYCR confirmed she has served on its Youth Advisory Board since 2025, but said it does not fund UC Davis's program and referred supervision questions to the county.

What we know

UC Davis said she joined Underground Scholars in January 2025, worked 10 hours a week as a paid peer mentor as part of her court requirements, and served on OYCR's Youth Advisory Board, traveling to speak on juvenile justice issues. The university said she met all program requirements, was monitored by the courts, and was attending summer school near completion of her degree at the time of her arrest. UC Davis said 92 students were enrolled in the program in 2026, including 14 who graduated.

The university did not answer questions about her day-to-day supervision, including whether her required weekly meetings with Underground Scholars Director Gunner Johnson continued through July.

Oversight quietly killed

A bill meant to bring more transparency to the LRP system passed the state Senate 37-1 in May. It was held in the Assembly Appropriations Committee's suspense file Aug. 13 — killed without a floor vote or public explanation, a procedural mechanism lawmakers routinely use to quietly shelve legislation.

Assembly Appropriations Committee Chair Buffy Wicks, who controls what survives her committee, did not respond to questions about her decision to effectively kill the oversight bill there.

Similarly, Speaker Robert Rivas's office did not provide an on-the-record response.

What's next

This is the first story in an ongoing investigation. A full accounting will require contacting every campus running one of these three programs — roughly 20 CSU campuses, 8 or more UC campuses, and dozens of community colleges — individually, since no state agency compiles the numbers in one place. We're continuing that work.

World.title: Pilot reports possible burn injuries after passenger's laptop catches fire
World.content:
A passenger's laptop caught fire on an American Airlines flight Friday, with the pilot reporting that some passengers may have been burned, according to air traffic control audio.

One passenger was treated and released after American Airlines Flight 2398 landed at Dallas Fort Worth International Airport, the airport said in a statement.

"Cabin fire in the back of the airplane," the pilot says in air traffic control audio obtained by CBS News. "The flight attendants are trying to put it out now."

The flight, which originated in Atlanta, had 133 people on board, the pilot told air traffic controllers.

"I think we have about four to five passengers that were burned by the laptop," the pilot says. "The laptop is contained about mid-aircraft."

"American Airlines flight 2398 landed safely at DFW after reports of smoke from a customer's device during landing," American Airlines said in a statement. "We thank our crew for their professionalism and swift response to quickly contain the device."

CBS News has reached out to the Federal Aviation Administration for comment.

The lithium batteries used in devices such as laptops and cellphones can pose risks on flights due to overheating, according to the FAA, because of a process known as "thermal runaway."

"Thermal runaway can occur without warning as a result of various factors, including if the battery is damaged, overheated, exposed to water, overcharged, or improperly packed," the FAA says in an advisory.

The FAA has size limits for lithium batteries on flights because of those risks.

So far this year, there have been at least 56 lithium battery incidents reported on flights that involved smoke, fire or overheating, per FAA data.

In February, an Alaska Airlines flight bound for Wichita, Kansas, was forced to return to Seattle, Washington, after a passenger's power bank device overheated and caught fire.

World.title: Men describe being deported by U.S. to dangerous African nation: "We cannot leave"
World.content:
Last year, Cuban immigrant Yasmany Moreno de Armas was working and living in Florida. He's now in the Central African Republic, after the Trump administration sent him and dozens of deportees to the deeply impoverished and conflict-ridden nation.

The 31-year-old said he only learned the U.S. government was deporting him to Africa after he arrived there in late July, alongside detainees from countries across the globe, including Ecuador, Honduras, Serbia, Russia and Vietnam.

"We cannot leave, we don't have documents and we're suffering and missing our families, in a continent we don't know," Moreno de Armas told CBS News in Spanish over a video call from inside a building in Bangui, the country's capital, where the deportees have been living.

Asked if he had ever heard of the Central African Republic prior to his deportation, he said "never."

The Central African Republic is one of the poorest countries in the world. Armed conflict, political instability and Russian mercenaries have also made it one of the most dangerous. The State Department warns Americans through a Level 4 travel advisory not to visit the country, citing the widespread insecurity there.

The landlocked nation is one of more than 30 countries the U.S. government has convinced to accept third-country deportees arrested as part of President Trump's large-scale crackdown on illegal immigration. The list includes a growing number of African countries, many of which are plagued by armed conflict, repressive governments and human rights abuses.

Eritrea native Zena Gebrgzabher, 39, is also stranded in the Central African Republic after being ejected from the U.S.

"I miss my family," Gebrgzabher told CBS News over a video call.

"My son. He asked like every day to my wife, '(where) is my daddy?'" he added.

Gebrgzabher's wife and their 5-year-old son, both of whom are American citizens, live in Maryland, where he said he worked as a truck driver. Like Moreno de Armas, Gebrgzabher said he was not given any notice of his deportation to the Central African Republic or allowed to challenge it.

Yrgalem Gehrehiwet called her husband's deportation unfair and inhumane. She said their son, Nathan, has been particularly affected by his father's absence, though she has refrained from telling him about Gebrgzabher's predicament.

"More than us because he loves his dad," she told CBS News.

CBS News could not find any criminal record for Moreno de Armas or Gebrgzabher, beyond traffic and immigration violations, like entering the U.S. illegally. But both men's cases do match the description of many of those targeted by the Trump administration for deportation to far-flung "third countries."

For the most part, the Trump administration has sought to use third-country deportation agreements to deport immigrants whose home countries, like Cuba, reject or limit U.S. deportations or who have won legal protections in U.S. immigration courts that shield them from being returned to their homelands due to concerns about their safety.

The Department of Homeland Security did not immediately respond to questions about the men sent to the Central African Republic and the nature of its agreement with that country, including what it is getting for accepting deportees from the U.S.

Moreno de Armas said he could be in danger in Cuba, since he was once imprisoned there after his first attempt to flee the communist-ruled island. Cuban government documents show he was imprisoned for "illegal exit from the national territory." His second attempt proved successful.

U.S. government documents show he arrived in Florida by boat in September 2016 and was allowed into the U.S. under the "parole" legal authority that Cuban arrivals benefited from under the now-defunct "Wet Foot, Dry Foot" policy. He applied for a green card under the Cold War-era Cuban Adjustment Act, but was denied on the grounds that he filed the application after his parole expired.

Lacking legal status, Moreno de Armas was arrested by immigration officials in May 2025 and spent roughly a year in Immigration and Customs Enforcement custody before his deportation to Africa this summer.

Gebrgzabher won his legal case in immigration court in 2017, when an immigration judge found him eligible for protection under the Convention Against Torture and barred his deportation to Eritrea.

Court documents show Gebrgzabher did not get asylum, a more permanent legal status, because he served as a checkpoint guard in the Eritrean military. Even though judges noted he was forcibly conscripted as an 18-year-old, they found him to be ineligible for asylum because of a rule that disqualifies those who may have assisted in the persecution of others. While he said he did not harm or arrest anyone passing through the checkpoint, the judges said he impeded the escape of political prisoners.

The documents indicate Gebrgzabher was imprisoned by the Eritrean military after overstaying his leave, and subsequently fled the country. He then traveled to the U.S.-Mexico border, where he requested asylum at a port of entry.

After being granted protection under the Convention Against Torture, Gebrgzabher said he started a family and checked in with ICE regularly, without incident, until he was arrested during an appointment last year. While his protection barred his deportation to Eritrea, it did not legally prevent officials from sending him to a third country like the Central African Republic.

Both men CBS News spoke to described being effectively stateless, stuck in a foreign nation where they don't speak the language and lack any ties or relatives.

"If you're going to be deported, it should be to your home country, not to another country where you don't know the culture," Moreno de Armas said.

World.title: Trump threatens defamation suit against left-leaning think tank
World.content:
President Trump's legal team is threatening to sue left-leaning think tank Center for American Progress for defamation over a report it issued in July that found "no evidence that National Guard deployments have reduced violent crime."

In an Aug. 17 letter, Mr. Trump's lawyer, Alejandro Brito, claimed the report contains materially false statements intended to damage the president. He set a deadline of 5 p.m. Friday for the organization to retract the report, apologize and compensate the president. Failure to comply, Brito wrote, could result in a lawsuit seeking at least $5 billion in damages.

Kevin Metz, an attorney for the Center for American Progress, responded in a letter: "This is utterly absurd: truth is not and cannot be defamation. … The right to disagree with the government, debate policies, and express dissent over policy choices is central to a functioning American democracy."

Both letters were obtained by CBS News. CBS News has reached out to Brito for comment.

"This threatened lawsuit's attack on facts and evidence is baseless," CAP President and CEO Neera Tanden said in a statement. "A fundamental protection of the First Amendment is to allow for the publication of facts and analysis that are contrary to the arguments and claims of any administration. A lawsuit is a transparent attempt to silence us. We will neither cower nor bend in the face of it."

The Trump administration first deployed National Guard troops to Los Angeles in June 2025 with a mission to protect federal immigration officials and other federal law enforcement amid heated protests over immigration raids.

Two months later, Mr. Trump announced Guard troops would also deploy to Washington, D.C., "to rescue our nation's capital from crime, bloodshed, bedlam and squalor and worse." Deployments to Memphis and New Orleans followed.

The report that drew the president's ire relied on multiple analyses of citywide crime data in those communities and concluded that the National Guard deployments "had no measurable effect on violent crime, homicides, or gun victimizations."

Overall, the FBI reported last week that violent crime rates were down nationwide in 2025.

If Mr. Trump pursues a lawsuit over CAP's report, he's "going to have a difficult hill to climb because of the legal standard that is used by public figures in defamation cases," said CBS News legal contributor Jessica Levinson, a professor at Loyola Law School in Los Angeles.

"The official has to show that the defendant made the statement at issue with actual malice, which means they knew the statement was false, or they acted in reckless disregard of its falsity," Levinson explained.

"It's very unlikely that a dispute about statistics would give rise to a defamation claim."

In addition, she said, the president "would have to show that the statements of issue are reasonably understood as being about him, as opposed to statements ... generally criticizing his administration."

Mr. Trump has a history of using lawsuits to target institutions and individuals he perceives as political opponents.

Tanden, in her statement, said, "In America, profound disagreements over public policy are resolved through robust public debate, not through threats or intimidation. Independent data, evidence, and analysis are essential to that debate. Efforts to silence independent research because its findings are unwelcome by an administration or president should alarm every American."

World.title: U.S.-Canada trade talks collapse just before deadline for tariffs
World.content:
U.S.-Canada trade talks collapse just before deadline for tariffs

toggle caption Manuel Balce Ceneta/AP

Trade negotiations between the United States and Canada fell apart on Friday night, shortly before a midnight deadline for 50% tariffs to take effect on $20 billion worth of Canadian products.

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said in a statement, shared on social media late Friday, that "Canada will match those tariffs dollar for dollar to protect our workers and businesses."

Carney said important progress had been made in recent weeks toward "improving Canada's position as having the best deal in the world with the U.S." That progress, however, did not meet Canada's objectives, he said, adding: "As a result, this evening, I have decided to suspend trade negotiations with the U.S. and have directed negotiators to return to Ottawa."

Sponsor Message

The prime minister blamed the U.S. for the collapse in negotiations. "Last-minute changes in the U.S. proposed terms were unfair, uneconomic, and called into question the reliability of any deal," Carney said, concluding, "Canada has what the world wants. And we will not allow any nation to determine our future."

Shortly after midnight, U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer responded to Carney with a statement posted on social media saying Canada had "declined to finalize the trade deal under the terms agreed earlier this week."

"Despite the U.S. offer to Canada to receive the best treatment of any major exporter to our market, new demands and walk backs of other commitments by Canada have upended the careful balance reached in the past days," Greer said.

He added that earlier this week "the United States agreed to provide even better treatment to Canada, offering significant tariff reductions on steel, aluminum, autos, and lumber."

"The offer would have led to supply chain coordination on aerospace, complementary actions to address unfair trade practices, critical minerals cooperation, increased enforcement against imports produced with forced labor, and the announcement of formal U.S.-Mexico-Canada Agreement (USMCA) negotiations," Greer said in his statement.
