World.title: Extradited Navy offficer, accused of fuel-trafficking, arrives from Argentina to Mexico’s top security prison
World.content:
Alleged fuel smuggler Rear Admiral Fernando Farías Laguna arrived from Argentina on Friday and is now incarcerated at the Altiplano maximum security prison in México state.

Farías — accused of leading a network that siphoned off millions in profits from state oil company Pemex — will face an initial arraignment hearing ahead of what promises to be explosive judicial proceedings.

Fernando “N”, posiblemente relacionado con una compleja red criminal dedicada al contrabando, dispersión y distribución de combustible, es trasladado a México. pic.twitter.com/A96Bh8ToZt — FGR México (@FGRMexico) August 20, 2026

After months on the run, Farías was arrested in Buenos Aires in April for entering Argentina with a fake passport. Two petitions for asylum were rejected and his challenges against extradition were turned aside. His departure has been categorized as an administrative expulsion.

His brother Manuel Roberto Farías Laguna, a former vice admiral, has been in prison since September 2025. The sibling high-ranking Navy officers allegedly ran a corruption network across several customs posts.

The network was finally exposed in March 2025 and federal authorities swept up 14 suspects — including Manuel Roberto — six months later.

Further heightening the intrigue, the Farías Laguna were nephews of Admiral Rafael Ojeda Durán, the Navy minister during the Andrés Manuel López Obrador administration (2018-2024).

A rear admiral who had reported the scheme to Admiral Ojeda in June 2024 was murdered in November of that year under mysterious circumstances.

Then-Attorney General Alejandro Gertz defended Ojeda’s integrity, saying the admiral himself had approached the authorities to request an investigation into some of the naval officers assigned to custom posts, although no evidence of any such investigation was made public.

The Farías Laguna case has dealt a serious blow to the reputation of the Navy, which had long been considered more disciplined and more reliable than the Army, which has dealt with its fair share of corruption scandals and allegations of human‑rights abuses.

The FGR has built its case against the Farías brothers with testimony from a protected witness known as “Santo,” who claims the suspects controlled the appointment of subordinates in customs offices (which are controlled by the Navy) and paid them substantial bribes.

Once the case goes to trial, Fernando Farías’s defense counsel is expected to summon Ojeda and argue that Farías was a subordinate in the corruption network. The defense is likely to add further fuel to the fire by alluding to allegations that Andrés Manuel López Beltrán — the son of the former president — is linked to the smuggling network.

President Claudia Sheinbaum this week rejected the suggestion that López Beltrán was involved in criminal activity.

The defense has also argued that the United States improperly intervened in Farías’s expulsion from Argentina.

With reports from La Jornada, EFE, El País and SDP Noticias

World.title: Mexico rejects US decision to deport Mexicans to Central America: Friday’s mañanera recapped
World.content:
Listen to this article

Today’s mañanera in 60 seconds

🌡️ Sheinbaum sits out press conference: Early on Friday, the president announced she woke up with “very bad flu, cough and fever” and was told by doctors to rest. Interior Minister Rosa Icela Rodríguez and INAH chief Joel Omar Vázquez led the conference in her place. Sheinbaum said she expected to resume activities the next day.

Early on Friday, the president announced she woke up with “very bad flu, cough and fever” and was told by doctors to rest. Interior Minister Rosa Icela Rodríguez and INAH chief Joel Omar Vázquez led the conference in her place. Sheinbaum said she expected to resume activities the next day. 🏺 INAH reveals discoveries in Chiapas cave: Vázquez said archaeologists found 13 offerings and 179 pre-Hispanic pieces this year in the Mundo Zoque cave, a Zoque pilgrimage site used to request rain and good harvests. Highlights include ceramics from the late Classic Period (600–900 AD) and an incense burner featuring a quincunx design.

Vázquez said archaeologists found 13 offerings and 179 pre-Hispanic pieces this year in the Mundo Zoque cave, a Zoque pilgrimage site used to request rain and good harvests. Highlights include ceramics from the late Classic Period (600–900 AD) and an incense burner featuring a quincunx design. 🇺🇸 🛬 Mexico objects to deportations to Central America: Rodríguez said she told U.S. Ambassador Ronald Johnson that Mexico disagrees with Washington’s decision to send some Mexican deportees to Central America rather than Mexico.

Rodríguez said she told U.S. Ambassador Ronald Johnson that Mexico disagrees with Washington’s decision to send some Mexican deportees to Central America rather than Mexico. 📈 Rodríguez touts July growth data: The interior minister called INEGI’s preliminary estimate of 2.7% annual GDP growth in July “yet another piece of good news,” following 2.1% growth in Q2.

Why today’s mañanera matters

At 6:01 a.m. Friday, President Claudia Sheinbaum announced on social media that she had woken up with “very bad flu, cough and fever.”

“It’s nothing serious, but doctors have recommended rest, so today’s [press] conference will be organized by Interior Minister Rosa Icela Rodríguez Velázquez and the general director of the National Institute of Anthropology and History, Joel Omar Vázquez Herrera,” she wrote.

Les informo que amanecí con gripa muy fuerte, tos y fiebre; no es nada grave, pero los médicos me han recomendado reposo, por lo que la conferencia de hoy estará coordinada por la secretaria de Gobernación, Rosa Icela Rodríguez Velázquez, y el director general del INAH, Joel Omar… — Claudia Sheinbaum Pardo (@Claudiashein) August 21, 2026

“Don’t miss it, they will talk about archaeological discoveries. I’m sure that tomorrow I’ll resume my activities. An affectionate hug from afar,” Sheinbaum wrote.

Later on Friday morning, Vázquez spoke about recent discoveries in a subterranean cave in the southern state of Chiapas.

Rodríguez subsequently provided a headline for media outlets by revealing that she had told U.S. Ambassador to Mexico Ronald Johnson that Mexico doesn’t agree with the Trump administration’s decision to send some Mexican deportees to Central America.

Also of note at today’s mañanera was the interior minister’s response to data showing that the Mexican economy performed solidly in July.

Discoveries in the ‘Mundo Zoque’ Cave

Vázquez spoke about discoveries archaeologists have made in the Mundo Zoque (Zoque World) Cave, a cave in the municipality of Cintalapa, Chiapas, that is named after the Indigenous Zoque people.

The cave, Vázquez explained, was a pilgrimage site where Zoque people went to “request rain and good harvests.”

The INAH chief said that in the first half of this year, archaeologists discovered 13 ofrendas (offerings) in the cave along with 179 pre-Hispanic pieces, including ceramic bowls.

Vázquez said that INAH has determined that the ceramic pieces were made in the late Classic Period — i.e. between 600 and 900 B.C. He said that the pieces include images of jaguars, tecolotes (a kind of owl), “human representations and plant motives.”

Vázquez highlighted that one of the pieces found by archaeologists is a sahumador (incense burner) with a 32-centimeter-long handle. The incense burner’s plate features “the image of a quincunx, a figure that alludes to the four directions of the universe,” he said, noting also that the end of the handle is adorned with a snake design.

“It’s a sublime piece, a very beautiful piece that is representative of the Zoque culture,” Vázquez said.

He said that archeologists also found stalactites and stalagmites in the cave that had been “modified to look like human figures or the jaws of the monster of the earth.”

Rodríguez: Mexico doesn’t agree with US decision to send Mexican deportees to Central America

Rodríguez told reporters that her meeting with Ambassador Johnson on Thursday focused on migration.

She said that she and the ambassador spoke about the reduction in “irregular migration” to the United States of both Mexicans and nationals of other countries.

“It has declined 96%,” Rodríguez said, apparently referring to the monthly average of illegal crossings during the Trump administration compared to the monthly average during the Biden administration.

The interior minister subsequently noted that the United States has deported some Mexicans to Central American countries.

The Trump administration has been quietly deporting migrants from Mexico to Honduras and Guatemala, despite the Mexican government’s willingness to accept the return of all its citizens, Homeland Security sources tell CBS News’ @camiloreports. pic.twitter.com/qe84ZJNpxi — CBS News (@CBSNews) August 19, 2026

As a result of “this new U.S. decision,” Mexicans have been sent to Guatemala, Honduras and Costa Rica, Rodríguez said. She said she told Johnson that Mexico respects the migration policy decisions of other countries, “but we don’t agree with our compatriots being sent to a third country.”

“… We spoke about this firmly, respectfully but firmly, in order to say that we don’t agree with this decision,” Rodríguez said.

Rodríguez celebrates solid economic growth in July

A reporter noted that INEGI published preliminary data showing that the Mexican economy grew 2.7% in annual terms in July. The publication of the data on Thursday came three weeks after INEGI reported annual growth of 2.1% in the second quarter of 2026. Annual growth in the first quarter was just 0.4%, and the Mexican economy contracted on a sequential basis in that period.

Rodríguez said that the growth data for July is “yet another piece of good news” for the Mexican economy.

“… It’s a very good indicator,” she said.

“… It’s another good result of the government of President Claudia Sheinbaum, and we’re going to continue on this same path,” Rodríguez said.

World.title: MND Local: New flights, fashion charity and Michin Aquarium in Guadalajara
World.content:
This week in Guadalajara, we look at the four new international routes being added at Miguel Hidalgo International Airport, the charitable activities of BRED and a great opportunity to visit the Michin Aquarium at a reduced cost.

While foreign airlines pull back, Volaris keeps expanding service in Guadalajara

We recently reported on Canadian carrier WestJet’s elimination of the new Guadalajara-Calgary nonstop route for the coming winter. Fortunately for Tapatíos, new routes will be arriving in its place starting in December.

The ultra-low-cost carrier (ULCC in industry jargon) will expand its service at Miguel Hidalgo International Airport this winter to the U.S. East Coast, along with two new international routes in Latin America.

Volaris’ new U.S. nonstop routes are from Atlanta’s Hartsfield-Jackson International Airport (ATL) and Washington Dulles International Airport (IAD). The carrier’s new southbound routes are to José María Córdova International Airport (MDE) in Medellín, Colombia, and La Aurora International Airport (GUA) in Guatemala City.

Three of those four flights are new nonstop routes for Guadalajara, the exception being the Atlanta route, already served by Delta Air Lines. The move cements Guadalajara as a strategic domestic hub for the airline. Volaris now services 60 destinations with more than 110 daily departures from Jalisco’s capital.

A growing network of connections

The new services reflect the Mexican carrier’s broader push to grow its U.S. network and increase its market share. Over the past year, Volaris has increased its U.S. network capacity by 12%, even as the overall market has contracted. From Guadalajara, Volaris offered 17.4% more seats in summer 2026 compared with summer 2025. Its rapid growth over this period drove its share of total capacity at GDL from 53% to nearly 60%.

Volaris’ new routes to Medellín and Guatemala City will provide meaningful improvement for southbound travel from Guadalajara, as the new routes eliminate the obligatory stop in Mexico City and should cut travel time in half. They are a welcome complement to Volaris’ existing nonstop service to Bogotá, Colombia, and San José, Costa Rica, from La Perla Tapatía.

BRED gives new life to the fashion industry’s mounds of unsold clothing

At the recently concluded Intermoda trade show for the fashion industry here in Guadalajara, local businessman Sergio López de la Cerda had more than the latest trends on his mind.

López de la Cerda was intent on making contacts and finding companies with excess goods to donate to the charitable organization he runs, The Clothing and Household Goods Bank of Guadalajara. Better known to locals as simply BRED, the organization’s mission is to distribute apparel, furniture and housewares to economically disadvantaged local families.

“What we are looking for is to link companies that manufacture clothing, that manufacture furniture or the marketers of these products, so that they can donate products to us, and we will take them directly to the families (who need it),” he told El Economista in a recent interview.

Leveraging a network of local textile, clothing, footwear and furniture producers, BRED is helping to reduce product waste while addressing a pressing social need.

Not the latest fashions, but fashions nonetheless

At Intermoda, López de la Cerda pointed out that many of the donated garments have no commercial value but are still perfectly usable. “Companies donate … clothing from a season that has already passed,” he explained.

If not for the involvement of social welfare groups, these unwanted goods would most likely end up in landfills. The silver lining for manufacturers and retailers is an opportunity to burnish their public image while reducing waste in their supply chains.

Clothing and household items collected by BRED are distributed through the logistics network of the Guadalajara Food Bank, which already had the infrastructure in place.

According to López de la Cerda, the organization now provides support to 338 communities in 81 municipalities in Jalisco, with regular donations of food, clothing, footwear, furniture and other basic items. It makes a meaningful contribution to helping improve the daily lives of an estimated 1.2 million Jalisco residents experiencing food insecurity.

BRED donation centers encourage public participation

To complement the goods donated by the business sector, BRED’s leadership seeks to boost citizen participation in its efforts. To this end, it operates more than 25 donation centers across the Guadalajara metropolitan area, where people can drop off clothing in good condition to help local families in need.

“We want families to bring in clothes they no longer use, as long as they are in good condition, so we can process them and send them directly to those who need them most,” López de la Cerda said.

Take the family on an underwater adventure without leaving the city

The Michin Aquarium is offering a deal to wrap up the summer season. From Aug. 14-30, 2026, entrance fees start at just 99 pesos per person, making a sea adventure accessible to those looking for affordable family fun right here in town.

Since 2017, the Michin Aquarium has been operating in Guadalajara’s historic center next to Alcalde Park. It houses approximately 10,000 marine organisms and serves as an important rescue, education and conservation center in western Mexico. The facility drew acclaim from conservationists back in 2018 as the first in Mexico to successfully breed neotropical river otters.

Popular exhibits include a vast oceanarium featuring bull sharks, nurse sharks and stingrays, which visitors experience up close by strolling through a glass tunnel. Additional exhibits showcase the variety of Mexican water habitats that are home to exotic jellyfish, technicolor reef fish, pink flamingos, crocodiles and more.

If that isn’t enough, a recently added petting zoo with capybaras and miniature pigs is sure to please the little ones.

Dates: The summer promotion runs Aug. 14-30, 2026.

Location: Calle Mariano Bárcena 990, Zona Centro, 44260 Guadalajara.

Cost: Tickets are available on the aquarium’s website, starting at 99 pesos.

MND Writer Dawn Stoner is reporting from Guadalajara.

World.title: Jamaica Rural Water Plan Puts US$50 Million to Work
World.content:
Jamaica · INFRASTRUCTURE

Key Facts — Funding US$35 million from the Caribbean Development Bank and US$15 million from Jamaica’s Consolidated Fund.

— Communities Agualta Vale, Mason Hall, Albert Town, Ulster Spring, Union, Balaclava, Port Morant, and Green Park.

— Duration The work will be rolled out over 18 months.

— Scope Includes water, sewerage, roads, and electricity in rural areas.

— Source The Jamaica Information Service reported the announcement on 21 August 2026.

A new US$50 million push will bring water, sewerage, roads and electricity to six rural communities across three parishes.

Illustrative photo: an outdoor tap. The US$50 million programme covers water, sewerage, roads and electricity in eight rural communities. (Photo: The Rio Times archive.)

The Government of Jamaica has announced a Jamaica rural water and infrastructure programme worth US$50 million. The funding will bring essential services to six rural communities across the island.

What the Jamaica Rural Water Plan Covers

The Caribbean Development Bank is putting in US$35 million. The other US$15 million comes from Jamaica’s Consolidated Fund.

The Caribbean Development Bank is a regional lender based in Barbados. The Consolidated Fund is the Jamaican government’s main account, financed by taxes and other revenue.

This combined funding will support a wide range of improvements in rural areas.

Where the Jamaica Rural Water Money Goes

Meanwhile, the programme will benefit communities in three parishes: St Mary, Trelawny, and St Elizabeth. The list runs to Agualta Vale and Mason Hall in St Mary, and Albert Town and Ulster Spring in Trelawny.

Union and Balaclava in St Elizabeth are also named. In addition, Port Morant in St Thomas and Green Park in St Ann are also included.

These eight communities will see improvements in water, sewerage, roads, and electricity.

Scope of Work

The Jamaica rural water programme will address water supply, sewerage systems, road conditions, and electricity infrastructure. This comprehensive approach aims to improve daily life in rural areas.

For example, reliable water and sewerage can boost public health, while better roads and electricity can support local businesses. The work will be carried out over an 18-month period.

Funding Sources

In addition, the Caribbean Development Bank is providing the majority of the funding, US$35 million. The remaining US$15 million comes from Jamaica’s Consolidated Fund, which is the government’s main revenue account.

This mix of regional and national financing reflects a shared commitment to rural development. The programme is a significant investment in Jamaica’s rural infrastructure.

Implementation Timeline

The rollout is scheduled to take place over 18 months. This timeframe allows for careful planning and execution of the various projects.

Meanwhile, residents can expect gradual improvements as the programme progresses. The duration ensures that each community receives the necessary attention.

Expected Benefits

As a result, the Jamaica rural water and infrastructure programme is expected to enhance the quality of life in rural communities. Access to clean water and proper sewerage can reduce health risks.

Moreover, improved roads and electricity can facilitate trade and connectivity. These upgrades are vital for sustainable development in rural Jamaica.

Regional Context

Jamaica is still repairing damage from Hurricane Melissa, the Category 5 storm that hit the island in late October 2025. Instead, it is a proactive investment in rural infrastructure.

The Caribbean Development Bank’s involvement highlights regional cooperation in development.

Community Impact

Overall, the selected communities range from coastal areas to inland towns. Each will receive tailored improvements to meet local needs.

For instance, Agualta Vale and Mason Hall are in St Mary, while Albert Town and Ulster Spring are in Trelawny. The programme aims to address the specific challenges of each area.

Looking Ahead

The Jamaica rural water programme is a clear sign of the government’s commitment to rural development. With funding secured, the next step is implementation.

Overall, this initiative promises to bring lasting benefits to thousands of residents. The 18-month rollout will be closely watched by communities and stakeholders alike.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the Jamaica rural water programme?

It is a US$50 million initiative to improve water, sewerage, roads, and electricity in rural communities. The funding comes from the Caribbean Development Bank and Jamaica’s Consolidated Fund.

Which communities are included in the programme?

The programme covers Agualta Vale and Mason Hall in St Mary, Albert Town and Ulster Spring in Trelawny. Union and Balaclava in St Elizabeth, Port Morant in St Thomas, and Green Park in St Ann.

How long will the programme take?

The work is scheduled to be rolled out over 18 months. This timeline allows for comprehensive improvements across all communities.

Who is funding the programme?

The Caribbean Development Bank provides US$35 million, and Jamaica’s Consolidated Fund provides US$15 million. The Consolidated Fund is the government’s main revenue account.

Sources: Jamaica Information Service; Caribbean Development Bank.

World.title: Banks Push to Lift the 12% Cap in Brazil Housing Credit
World.content:
Brazil · HOUSING

Key Facts — Current cap The 12% annual ceiling applies to SFH-qualified housing loans for properties up to 2.25 million reais.

— Talks Large mortgage lenders are negotiating with the central bank to revise the 12% cap, reported 19 August 2026

— Framework Launched October 2025; 80% of housing loan resources must follow SFH rules

— Warning Regulation director Gilneu Vivan called the 12% limit a challenge in periods of higher rates

— Status No formal proposal, consultation, or deadline exists to change the ceiling; it remains in force.

The cap stays in force, and the central bank’s own regulator has called it a challenge.

Apartment towers in Curitiba. The 12% cap applies to regulated housing loans on properties worth up to 2.25 million reais. (Photo: Mateusmatsuda, CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons.)

Large banks are pushing to lift the 12% cap in Brazil housing credit. Estadão and Valor International reported the talks on 19 August 2026.

The talks with the central bank aim to revise the ceiling in the new mortgage model. No formal proposal has been made.

Banks Seek to Revise Housing Credit Cap

Large mortgage-lending banks are negotiating with Brazil’s central bank to revise the 12% annual interest ceiling in the new mortgage model. Estadão and Valor International reported the talks on 19 August 2026.

However, no business association was named, and no formal petition or consultation was identified. The discussions appear to be informal, as the ceiling remains in force.

Understanding the 12% Cap in Housing Credit

The 12% cap is the maximum annual cost or interest rate banks may charge on SFH-qualified housing loans. Descriptions vary between total cost, meaning interest plus fees and commissions, and interest a year over the index.

In addition, the cap applies to properties worth up to 2.25 million reais, which rose from 1.5 million reais. This means more expensive homes are now eligible for regulated loans.

The New Housing Credit Framework

The new housing credit framework reallocates savings-deposit funding and increases the share of loans under the SFH, the Sistema Financeiro da Habitação. Under it, 80% of housing loan resources must follow SFH rules.

The government launched the model in October 2025, with gradual implementation from late 2025 and full implementation scheduled for January 2027. Meanwhile, banks can raise funds in capital markets under the framework.

How Banks Benefit From the Framework

If banks channel capital-market funds into mortgage lending, they get something back. They may use an equivalent amount of cheaper savings-deposit funding elsewhere for about six to seven years.

This is allowed provided 80% of housing credit operations comply with SFH rules. As a result, banks have an incentive to expand mortgage lending while managing their funding costs.

Still, the 12% cap limits how much they can charge on those loans.

Central Bank Official Warns on Cap

On 18 August 2026, at the ABECIP Summit, central bank regulation director Gilneu Vivan spoke publicly. He warned the 12% a year limit over the index could become a challenge when rates are higher.

He did not announce a rule change. Therefore, the warning signals potential pressure on the cap, but no decision has been made.

Even so, the ceiling remains in force for now.

Current Mortgage Rates in Brazil

Brazilian mortgage rates in 2026 run around 8.5% to 12% a year for fixed-rate loans. Floating products are at the TR index plus 8% to 10%, and FGTS-funded mortgages start near 8.5%.

For example, the 12% cap sits at the top of the typical fixed-rate range. By contrast, some loans are already near the ceiling, making any rise in rates a concern.

What Is the SFH and TR?

The SFH is Brazil’s regulated housing finance system, funded largely by savings deposits, with capped rates and property price limits. The TR is a reference rate used to index many Brazilian loans.

In short, the SFH aims to make housing credit accessible, while the TR helps adjust loan payments. These mechanisms are central to the new framework.

No Formal Proposal Yet

There is no formal proposal, consultation, draft rule, or deadline to change the ceiling. It remains in force, despite the ongoing talks.

Overall, the banks’ push is at an early stage. Consequently, borrowers should expect the 12% cap to stay for now.

Outlook for Housing Credit

The outcome of the negotiations could reshape housing credit in Brazil, especially if rates rise. However, any change would require a formal process, which has not started.

In the meantime, the cap continues to protect borrowers from higher costs. Still, banks may keep pressing for flexibility.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the 12% cap in Brazil housing credit?

The 12% cap is the maximum annual cost or interest rate banks may charge on SFH-qualified housing loans. It applies to properties worth up to 2.25 million reais.

Are banks formally asking to lift the cap?

No, there is no formal proposal, consultation, or draft rule. Large banks are negotiating with the central bank, but the talks are informal and the cap remains in force.

When was the new housing credit framework launched?

The government launched the model in October 2025, with gradual implementation from late 2025. Full implementation is scheduled for January 2027.

What did the central bank say about the cap?

Central bank regulation director Gilneu Vivan spoke on 18 August 2026. He warned the 12% limit could become a challenge when rates are higher.

Sources: Estadão; Valor International; Banco Central do Brasil.

World.title: Brazil Blocks Welfare Recipients From Betting Accounts
World.content:
Brazil · SOCIETY

Key Facts — Scope The restriction covers Bolsa Família and BPC beneficiaries, plus Desenrola Brasil and Fies borrowers.

— Enforcement Operators must close accounts within three days and return the balance.

— Checks Licensed operators must verify blocked CPFs at account opening, daily access, and every 15 days.

— Impact Reports cite 2.8 million, roughly 3 million, and about 5 million blocked CPFs in different groupings.

— Context In August 2024, beneficiaries transferred 3 billion reais to betting platforms, about 21% of that month’s transfers.

The rule, in force since July 2026, aims to stop welfare cash from flowing into online gambling.

The Esplanada dos Ministérios in Brasília. The Finance Ministry’s betting secretariat keeps the list of blocked taxpayer numbers. (Photo: Dasfour2022, CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons.)

One-stop reference Company Intelligence Every listed company in Latin America — financials, ownership and structure for 1,450+ companies across 26 exchanges, in one place. Browse the directory →

Brazil has moved to block welfare recipients from betting accounts, a measure that aims to keep social benefits out of online gambling. The rule took effect in July 2026.

It is enforced by the Ministry of Finance’s Secretariat of Prizes and Bets, the SPA.

What the Rule Does

The SPA blocks benefit recipients from opening or keeping betting accounts, matched by CPF, Brazil’s individual taxpayer number. Operators must close existing accounts within three days and return the balance.

In addition, licensed operators must check the SPA’s list of blocked CPFs. They check when a user opens an account, on the first daily access, and at least every 15 days after that.

If a person on the list is identified, the platform must close the account and refund the remaining funds.

Who Is Affected

The restriction covers Bolsa Família, Brazil’s main cash transfer programme for low-income families. It also covers the BPC, a monthly payment for elderly and disabled people with very low income.

An August 2026 government notice says it also applies to Desenrola Brasil beneficiaries and Fies borrowers. Therefore, the measure reaches a wide range of welfare recipients.

The SPA keeps a list of blocked CPFs, which is the individual taxpayer registry number every Brazilian adult has.

Why the Measure Exists

The policy follows reporting that welfare money was flowing into betting. A June 2026 report cited the Court of Accounts on August 2024.

Beneficiaries transferred the equivalent of 3 billion reais to betting platforms that month, about 21% of their total transfers. As a result, the Finance Ministry issued the rule in October 2025, and it applied from July 2026.

The ministry says the measure is already in force.

How Many People Are Blocked

The Finance Ministry said about 2.8 million beneficiaries were already blocked from betting platforms. Another August report put roughly 3 million Bolsa Família and BPC beneficiaries as blocked.

Other categories bring total blocked CPFs to about 5 million. However, these figures reflect different groupings and time frames.

In short, the exact number of affected individuals is not a single figure.

How the Checks Work

Licensed operators check the blocked list at three moments. On account opening, on the first daily access, and at least every 15 days after that.

This ensures that betting accounts do not remain active for welfare recipients. Once a person on the list is identified, the platform must close the account and refund the remaining funds.

Even so, the rule does not specify penalties for operators that fail to check.

What This Means for Betting Accounts

For welfare recipients, betting accounts are now off-limits, and existing ones must be closed within three days. This is a direct response to the flow of benefit money into online gambling.

Meanwhile, for betting operators, the rule adds a compliance layer. They must regularly check the SPA’s list to avoid holding accounts for blocked individuals.

Background on the Benefits

Bolsa Família is Brazil’s main cash transfer programme for low-income families, providing monthly support. The BPC is a separate payment for elderly and disabled people with very low income.

Both programmes are central to Brazil’s social safety net. The rule aims to protect these funds from being spent on gambling.

The Role of the CPF

A CPF is the individual taxpayer registry number every Brazilian adult has, used to identify people across banks, benefits and public services. The SPA uses this number to match welfare recipients with betting accounts.

Therefore, the CPF is the key tool for enforcing the ban. It allows the SPA to maintain a list of blocked individuals and ensure operators comply.

What Happens Next

The rule is already in force, and operators must comply with the three-day closure requirement. The SPA will continue to update its list of blocked CPFs.

In addition, the government may extend the restriction to other benefit categories in the future. For now, the focus remains on protecting welfare funds from betting accounts.

Frequently Asked Questions

What are betting accounts?

Betting accounts are online accounts that users open with licensed betting platforms to place wagers. In Brazil, these accounts are now restricted for welfare recipients.

Who is blocked from betting accounts?

Beneficiaries of Bolsa Família and the BPC are blocked, as are Desenrola Brasil beneficiaries and Fies borrowers. The SPA matches these individuals by their CPF.

How long do operators have to close accounts?

Operators must close existing betting accounts within three days and return the balance. They must also check the blocked list regularly to prevent new accounts.

Why did Brazil implement this rule?

The rule follows reports that welfare money was flowing into betting, with beneficiaries transferring 3 billion reais in August 2024. The measure aims to stop this flow and protect social benefits.

Sources: Ministério da Fazenda; Folha; Exame; O Globo.

World.title: Lula Asks Brussels to Save Brazil Chicken Exports
World.content:
Brazil · TRADE

Key Facts — Letter date President Lula wrote to European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen on 31 July 2026.

— EU action The EU removed Brazil from its list of authorised animal product exporters in May 2026.

— Effective date The delisting takes effect on 3 September 2026.

— Audit The Commission scheduled an audit in Brazil at the end of August 2026.

— Trade status The ban is a sanitary measure, not a suspension of the Mercosur-EU trade agreement.

The European Union’s ban on Brazilian poultry takes effect on 3 September 2026, but a scheduled audit may offer a path back.

The Berlaymont in Brussels, seat of the European Commission. Lula’s letter went to Commission President Ursula von der Leyen on 31 July 2026. (Photo: EmDee, CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons.)

Brazil chicken exports to the European Union are days from being cut off. President Lula has asked Brussels to restore Brazil to its export list for chicken and honey, provisionally.

The request came in a letter to European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, sent on 31 July 2026.

The Letter and Its Request

Lula wrote to von der Leyen on 31 July 2026. He asked that Brazil be restored, provisionally, to the EU list for chicken and honey.

This would last until EU audits of Brazil’s antimicrobial control system are complete. The letter was reported by Estãdao on 22 August 2026.

It seeks a temporary fix while the audits are pending.

Why the EU Delisted Brazil

The European Union removed Brazil from its list of third countries authorised to export products of animal origin. The reason was non-compliance with rules on antimicrobial growth promoters and related official controls.

Antimicrobial growth promoters are antibiotics given to healthy farm animals to make them grow faster. The EU banned this practice because it helps breed drug-resistant bacteria.

Timeline of the Ban

An EU committee made the delisting decision on 12 May 2026. The ban takes effect on 3 September 2026.

Until then, Brazil remains delisted, and the ban will apply as scheduled. Therefore, the window for action is narrow.

The Scheduled Audit

The Commission scheduled an audit in Brazil at the end of August 2026 to assess compliance on antimicrobial controls. It indicated that if results are positive, it may amend the list to restore Brazil’s eligibility, particularly for poultry and honey.

In addition, this audit could provide a path forward. However, no restoration has been agreed yet.

Impact on Brazil Chicken Exports

Brazil is one of the world’s largest exporters of chicken. Therefore, the ban could hit Brazil chicken exports significantly.

The letter aims to prevent a disruption in trade. Still, the outcome depends on the audit results.

Sanitary Measure, Not Trade Suspension

The ban is applied as a sanitary and animal health measure under EU law. It is not a suspension of the Mercosur and EU trade agreement.

That agreement remains formally in place. Meanwhile, market access for Brazilian animal products is blocked on health grounds.

What Happens Next

The audit at the end of August 2026 is the next key step. If results are positive, the EU may restore Brazil’s eligibility.

Even so, the ban takes effect on 3 September 2026 unless the list is amended before then. The letter seeks a provisional restoration to bridge this gap.

Broader Context for Brazil Chicken Exports

Brazil chicken exports are a major part of its agricultural trade. This dispute with the EU adds uncertainty for producers.

As a result, the government is seeking a diplomatic solution. The letter to Brussels is part of that effort.

Looking Ahead

The coming weeks will be crucial for Brazil chicken exports. The audit results will determine whether the EU changes its position.

In short, the ball is in Brussels’ court. The response to Lula’s letter and the audit will shape the future of this trade.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why did the EU ban Brazilian chicken?

The EU removed Brazil from its list of authorised exporters because of non-compliance with rules on antimicrobial growth promoters. These are antibiotics given to healthy animals to speed growth, which the EU bans to prevent drug-resistant bacteria.

When does the ban take effect?

The ban takes effect on 3 September 2026. The EU committee made the decision on 12 May 2026.

What is Lula asking for?

Lula asked that Brazil be restored provisionally to the EU list until audits are complete. He wrote to European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen on 31 July 2026.

Is the Mercosur-EU trade agreement suspended?

No, the agreement remains formally in place. The ban is a sanitary measure, not a trade suspension.

Sources: Estãdao; Reuters; Bloomberg; Agência Brasil.

World.title: Ghana Booked US$1.91 Billion of Investment. Only US$88 Million Was New
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

GHANA · INVESTMENT

Key Facts —The headline: Ghana registered US$2.62 billion of foreign direct investment across 254 projects in 2025. —The catch: On the Bank of Ghana’s balance-of-payments measure, net inflow was US$1.91 billion and 95.4% of it was reinvested earnings. —New money: That leaves roughly US$88 million of genuinely fresh capital entering the country. —China leads on count: China registered 70 projects, ahead of India with 22 and Nigeria with 10. —Cayman leads on value: The Cayman Islands ranked first by value at US$500.56 million, with China second at US$486.06 million. —Sectors: Manufacturing was most active with 99 projects worth US$368.71 million; mining services led by value with US$506.61 million from just three projects. —The forecast: The agency projects US$2.80 billion in 2026 and US$3.11 billion in 2027, before a dip to US$2.38 billion in the 2028 election year.

Ghana foreign direct investment came to US$2.62 billion in 2025, but the more revealing number sits in the central bank’s accounts. There, net inflow was US$1.91 billion and 95.4% of it was profit that companies already in Ghana chose to leave there.

Two numbers, two different things

The 2025 Annual Investment Report was compiled by Ghana’s investment promotion authority with the Bank of Ghana, the Petroleum Commission and the Ghana Free Zones Authority. Its headline figure is a registration number: US$2.62 billion across 254 approved projects, which the agency projects will create 18,748 jobs, plus US$816.05 million of wholly Ghanaian-owned investment.

The balance-of-payments figure is different, and it is the one comparable with international data. On that basis net foreign direct investment was US$1.91 billion.

The two measures diverge by about US$710 million, and the report does not reconcile them. Registration counts what was approved; the balance of payments counts what actually crossed the border.

What 95.4% reinvested earnings really means

Reinvested earnings are profits generated inside Ghana by foreign-owned firms and retained there rather than repatriated. They are legitimately counted as foreign direct investment, and they are a genuine vote of confidence.

They are not, however, new capital arriving from abroad. If 95.4% of a US$1.91 billion inflow is recycled profit, the fresh money entering Ghana in 2025 was on the order of US$88 million.

For a country rebuilding its credibility after a sovereign default, that distinction carries the whole report. Existing investors are staying and compounding; new ones are still watching.

Who is behind Ghana foreign direct investment

By project count China led with 70, well ahead of India on 22 and Nigeria on 10. That is a familiar pattern across West Africa, where Chinese firms arrive in volume at the smaller end of the ticket range.

By value the ranking inverts. The Cayman Islands came first at US$500.56 million, with China second at US$486.06 million.

The Cayman number should be read as a conduit rather than a source. It tells you where the holding company is registered, not who ultimately owns the money.

Manufacturing was the most active sector with 99 projects worth US$368.71 million, while mining services topped the value table with US$506.61 million from only three projects. Greater Accra absorbed 143 projects worth US$619.37 million.

Why the distinction is not academic

Ghana defaulted on its external debt in December 2022 and has spent the years since negotiating its way back. Every restructuring signature, and there was another with Belgium this week, is aimed at the same audience: capital that has not yet come back.

A country in that position needs new entrants, not just loyal incumbents. Reinvested earnings keep existing plants running and existing payrolls paid, but they do not add factories, ports or wells.

The macro backdrop the report cites is genuinely better, with growth of 6.0% in 2025 and inflation at 5.4% in December. That is the sort of picture that should be pulling in first-time investors.

It has not yet. The gap between a good macro story and about US$88 million of fresh capital is the single most useful thing in this report, and the report itself does not draw attention to it.

The pipeline, and what to discount

The agency tracks US$11.48 billion of announced but unbuilt projects. Three of them account for US$8 billion: a US$5 billion fertiliser plant, a US$2 billion Jubilee and TEN oilfield agreement and a US$1 billion artificial-intelligence hub with the United Arab Emirates.

Its own forecasts are US$2.80 billion for 2026, US$3.11 billion for 2027 and US$2.38 billion for 2028, which the report notes is an election year. No methodology is published.

None of the three has a published financial close, and the remaining US$3.48 billion of the pipeline has no named counterparty at all. The report is also the promotion agency assessing its own performance.

Frequently Asked Questions

How much foreign direct investment did Ghana attract in 2025? Ghana registered US$2.62 billion across 254 projects. On the Bank of Ghana’s balance-of-payments measure, net inflow was US$1.91 billion. Why does the 95.4% figure matter? Because 95.4% of the balance-of-payments inflow was reinvested earnings from firms already operating in Ghana. That leaves roughly US$88 million of genuinely new capital. Which country invested most in Ghana? China led on project count with 70. By value the Cayman Islands ranked first at US$500.56 million, with China second at US$486.06 million. Which sectors drew the most investment? Manufacturing was most active with 99 projects worth US$368.71 million. Mining services led by value at US$506.61 million from three projects.

World.title: Morocco Votes on 23 September, and Candidates Register Online First
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

MOROCCO · POLITICS

Key Facts —Polling day: Wednesday 23 September 2026, fixed by decree 2.26.190 and published in the Bulletin Officiel. —Filed online: Candidacies go through an online platform that opens at 8 am on Monday 31 August. Paper originals must still be lodged in person. —Two deadlines: The platform closes at noon on Tuesday 8 September; the physical filing window runs a day longer, to noon on Wednesday 9 September. —The campaign: Official campaigning runs from the first minute of Thursday 10 September until the end of Tuesday 22 September. —The prize: 395 seats in the Chamber of Representatives, 305 from local constituencies and 90 from regional lists reserved in part for women. —The incumbent: Aziz Akhannouch has led the government since 2021, when his RNI took 102 seats and the Islamist PJD fell from 125 to 13.

Morocco will hold its general election on Wednesday 23 September 2026, with the campaign starting on 10 September. What is new about this Morocco election is the paperwork, because candidacies are being filed online for the first time.

What the decree actually sets out

The calendar comes from decree 2.26.190, presented by Interior Minister Abdelouafi Laftit and adopted by the government council on 5 March 2026. It was issued on 12 March and published in the Bulletin Officiel, and it rests on organic law 27.11 governing the Chamber of Representatives.

Candidates may begin filing online at 8 am on Monday 31 August. That platform closes at noon on Tuesday 8 September.

The physical window opens on the same morning and closes a day later, at noon on Wednesday 9 September. Local candidacies are lodged at prefecture or province headquarters, regional lists at the wilaya.

Official campaigning then runs from the first minute of Thursday 10 September until the end of Tuesday 22 September, the eve of the vote.

Why the online filing matters more than it sounds

Moroccan officials present this as the first general election in which candidacies are lodged digitally, and the two-stage deadline is why the platform shuts a full day early. List agents who file electronically then carry the paper originals to the authority at the slot printed on their provisional receipt.

An electronic filing on its own is not a valid candidacy. A receipt-holder who misses the appointment has to pull a new provisional receipt with a new sequence number.

For a system that has historically turned on the mechanics of list-building, that is not administrative trivia. It is a new way to lose a seat before a single vote is cast.

The arithmetic that decides the Morocco election

The Chamber of Representatives has 395 seats. Reporting on the structure puts 305 of them in 92 multi-member local constituencies and 90 in twelve region-based constituencies, with at least a third of the regional places going to women, placed first and second on each list.

A majority is 198. No party has come close to that on its own in the modern era, so the real contest is over who assembles the coalition.

The 2021 reform removed the old electoral threshold and shifted seat allocation to a quotient computed from registered voters rather than votes cast. Most analysts of that result attribute the bulk of the PJD collapse, from 125 seats to 13, to the new formula.

Whether the 2026 organic law altered that formula could not be established from the published texts. It is the technical question that will decide how fragmented the next chamber is.

What the last result tells you

In September 2021 the RNI took 102 seats, a gain of 65, and Aziz Akhannouch became head of government. The PAM took 87, down 15, and Istiqlal 81, up 35.

The collapse was the Islamist PJD, which fell from 125 seats to 13. It had led the two previous governments.

That was not a swing in public mood on the scale the numbers suggest. On the usual reading it was the new seat-allocation formula doing its work on a party whose support was broad but rarely dominant in any single constituency.

Which is why the technical questions about the 2026 rules are worth more attention than the campaign rhetoric. In Morocco, the counting method has recently mattered more than the count.

What is at stake for investors

Morocco is not a swing story for global capital, and that is rather the point. It has spent a decade building an export manufacturing base in cars, aerospace and electronics, and continuity is what foreign investors are pricing.

The 2021 result gave Akhannouch a stable three-party coalition. A messier 2026 chamber would not change Morocco’s industrial strategy overnight, but it would slow the decisions that sit behind it.

Those decisions are large. They include the phosphate build-out, the Atlantic gas pipeline project taken to Washington in July, and a port and logistics expansion that now competes directly with southern European transhipment hubs.

Frequently Asked Questions

When is the Morocco election in 2026? Polling day is Wednesday 23 September 2026, fixed by decree 2.26.190. Official campaigning runs from 10 September to midnight on 22 September. How do candidates register? Candidacies open online at 8 am on Monday 31 August and the platform closes at noon on Tuesday 8 September. Paper originals must then be filed in person by noon on Wednesday 9 September. How many seats are being contested? The Chamber of Representatives has 395 seats, reported as 305 from local constituencies and 90 from regional lists. A majority is 198. Who is the incumbent head of government? Aziz Akhannouch of the RNI, appointed after the September 2021 election in which his party won 102 seats. He remained in post as of August 2026.

World.title: Tanzania Paid US$2.8 Billion for Its Biggest Dam. Egypt Built It
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

EGYPT · GEOPOLITICS

Key Facts —The plant: The Julius Nyerere scheme on the Rufiji River generates 2,115 megawatts, making it Tanzania’s largest single power project. —Who paid: Tanzania financed it from its own budget at a stated cost of Sh7.452 trillion, about US$2.8 billion. —Who built it: An Egyptian consortium of Arab Contractors and Elsewedy Electric, from June 2019 to completion in March 2025. —Already running: By 31 May 2026 the plant had supplied about 44.9% of the electricity fed into the national grid over the preceding year. —The ceremony: President Samia Suluhu Hassan inaugurated it on Saturday 22 August at the site in Rufiji District, Coast Region. —The message: Egypt’s Prime Minister Mostafa Madbouly attended and said the project refutes claims that Egypt opposes development in Nile Basin countries. —The backdrop: Ethiopia said on 20 August it would build further dams whenever it deemed necessary, a day after Egypt’s foreign minister said Cairo would not allow more dams on the Nile.

Tanzania inaugurated the 2,115-megawatt Julius Nyerere hydropower plant on Saturday, a project it paid for itself and an Egyptian consortium built. Cairo is treating the result as an argument as much as an asset.

What Egypt actually delivered

The scheme sits on the Rufiji River in Rufiji District, Coast Region, inland from Dar es Salaam, and generates 2,115 megawatts across nine turbines. That makes it comfortably the largest generating asset in the country.

It was built by an Egyptian consortium of Arab Contractors and Elsewedy Electric, two firms that have spent the past decade turning Egyptian engineering capacity into an export business. Construction began in June 2019 and was completed in March 2025.

The important point about the money is that it was Tanzanian. The government puts the cost at Sh7.452 trillion, about US$2.8 billion at the shilling’s late-August rate, and financed it from its own budget rather than through a foreign loan.

About 12,000 people worked on the site, of whom 1,700 were Egyptian engineers and technicians, according to the Egyptian government. President Samia Suluhu Hassan led Saturday’s ceremony at the site.

The Nile argument the Julius Nyerere hydropower plant is meant to settle

Egypt’s Prime Minister Mostafa Madbouly flew in for the ceremony on behalf of President Abdel Fattah El-Sisi, and the line he chose was aimed squarely at Addis Ababa. He said the project refutes previous claims that Egypt opposes development in Nile Basin countries, while insisting Cairo will safeguard its rights in the river.

The timing was not accidental. On 20 August, Ethiopia’s water and energy minister Habtamu Itefa said his country would build further dams whenever it judged them necessary.

A day before that, Egyptian Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty said on television that Cairo would not allow the construction of additional dams on the Nile. The two statements sit about as far apart as two governments can manage while still nominally negotiating.

Talks among Egypt, Ethiopia and Sudan over the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam have been frozen since 2024. The Nile basin is shared by eleven countries, and Egypt has spent years losing the argument that its historic allocation should hold.

Why building somebody else’s dam is a strategy

For most of the past fifteen years Egypt’s Nile diplomacy has been defensive, and it has not worked. Ethiopia built the GERD anyway, and the rest of the basin largely sided with the upstream case.

Building 2.1 gigawatts for an upstream basin state is a different kind of argument. It is harder to accuse a country of blocking African development while its contractors are commissioning the largest power station in Tanzania.

There is a commercial dimension as well. Arab Contractors and Elsewedy Electric are becoming genuine pan-African engineering, procurement and construction players, and their order books are one of the more overlooked Egyptian export stories.

Egyptian contractors as an export industry

Elsewedy Electric began as a cable manufacturer and has spent two decades moving up the value chain into transmission, substations and turnkey power projects. Arab Contractors is one of the oldest construction houses in the Arab world and has worked across Africa since the 1970s.

Between them they now bid for the kind of work that used to go automatically to European, Chinese or Turkish firms. Tanzania is the largest single demonstration of that capability so far.

For Egypt the appeal is straightforward. Engineering exports earn hard currency, build political relationships that outlast any single government, and do not require Cairo to win a legal argument about water rights.

The limitation should be equally clear. A contractor delivers what a client finances, and here the client was Tanzania, which chose the Egyptians and wrote the cheques.

What it means for Tanzania

Saturday was a formal inauguration rather than a switch-on, and the distinction matters. The turbines have been feeding the grid progressively, and by 31 May the plant had supplied about 44.9% of all the electricity delivered to the national network over the preceding year.

Total installed capacity in Tanzania has now reached roughly 4,646 megawatts, of which this single site is 2,115. That is a level of concentration few countries would choose.

The country has spent 2026 courting large energy capital, from the long-delayed liquefied natural gas project to the Tanga corridor. Reliable baseload is the precondition for most of it.

One caution belongs on the record, and it is the usual one with large hydro. The Rufiji is a seasonal river, so a plant supplying nearly half the national grid ties the country’s electricity to the rains.

Frequently Asked Questions

How big is the Julius Nyerere hydropower plant? It generates 2,115 megawatts, which makes it Tanzania’s largest single power project. It sits on the Rufiji River in Rufiji District, Coast Region. Who built it and who paid? An Egyptian consortium of Arab Contractors and Elsewedy Electric built it between June 2019 and March 2025. Tanzania financed it from its own budget at a stated Sh7.452 trillion, about US$2.8 billion. Why is Egypt highlighting the project? Prime Minister Mostafa Madbouly said it refutes claims that Egypt opposes development in Nile Basin countries. The statement came days after Ethiopia said it would build more dams as needed. Are the GERD talks still running? No. Negotiations among Egypt, Ethiopia and Sudan over the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam have been frozen since 2024.

NIGERIA · MARKETS

Key Facts —The record: Domestic investors traded N10.68 trillion in the first seven months of 2026, or 89.21% of all activity on the Nigerian Exchange. —Foreigners: Foreign transactions came to N1.29 trillion, 10.79% of the total. —Already past last year: Seven months of domestic trading exceed the whole of 2025 by 15.21%. —The sell-off: The All-Share Index fell for an eighth consecutive session on 20 August, to 240,037.80 points. —The damage: Between 10 and 20 August the index lost 3.42% and market value fell N5.44 trillion, about US$4.0 billion, to N154.98 trillion. —Still up on the year: Despite the slide the index is ahead 54.3% so far in 2026.

Nigeria stock market domestic investors accounted for 89.21% of all trading on the Nigerian Exchange in the first seven months of 2026, a record, while foreign money supplied just 10.79%. The index has now fallen for eight sessions in a row.

The number that defines the market

The exchange’s own domestic and foreign portfolio investment report puts local transactions at N10.68 trillion between January and July, against N1.29 trillion from abroad. On the naira rate the central bank published for 20 August, that is roughly US$7.9 billion against US$957 million.

Seven months of domestic activity have already beaten the full year 2025, when local investors traded N9.27 trillion, by 15.21%. Nigeria’s biggest equity market is now, in turnover terms, overwhelmingly a domestic affair.

One caveat matters, and it cuts the other way. Foreign turnover of N1.29 trillion in seven months annualises to about N2.21 trillion against N2.65 trillion for the whole of 2025, so the domestic share rose because local volume nearly doubled, not because overseas money grew.

What Nigeria stock market domestic investors have been doing lately

Mostly selling. The All-Share Index closed at 240,037.80 points on Thursday 20 August, down 0.30% on the day and down for an eighth consecutive session.

Market capitalisation slipped to N154.98 trillion from N155.42 trillion, a fall of about N440 billion, or US$327 million, in one day. Fourteen stocks rose and twenty-eight fell.

Measured from Monday 10 August, the index is down 3.42% from 248,529.75 points and market value has fallen N5.44 trillion, or about US$4.0 billion, from N160.42 trillion.

Volume tells its own story. Some 2.87 billion shares changed hands, up 140.65%, on a value of only N33.99 billion, down 10.11%, which is the signature of heavy trading in cheap stocks.

Where the losses landed

Aradel Holdings was the single biggest drag, down 5.40% to N1,300.00 from N1,374.20. The NGX Oil and Gas index fell 2.49% to 4,837.50.

The banks were softer rather than broken. UBA lost 2.17% to N45.00, Zenith 0.48% to N123.40 and GTCO 0.23% to N127.60.

Insurance fell 0.79% and banking 0.41%. This is a broad drift, not a sector rout.

The 2007 to 2025 series, and why to distrust it

The exchange’s own report says domestic transactions rose 160.83% between 2007 and 2025, from N3.56 trillion to N9.27 trillion, while foreign transactions rose 329.87% from N0.62 trillion to N2.65 trillion. Those percentages are worth treating gently.

All of it is nominal naira, and the currency has been devalued heavily since 2023. A series that does not adjust for that is describing the unit of account as much as the market.

The report also contains a decade table whose figures do not sit comfortably with the 2007 base. Where two series inside one document disagree, the safe course is to use neither for a trend claim.

What survives the scepticism is the ratio, and the ratio is unambiguous. Nine out of every ten naira traded this year came from inside Nigeria.

Why a domestic market is not automatically a safer one

A market that no longer depends on foreign flows is insulated from one kind of shock. It is also, by definition, dependent on a much smaller pool of savings.

The same domestic base that set the record is the one now selling. When local institutions rebalance, there is no offsetting foreign bid to absorb it.

Exchange chief executive Temi Popoola has said capitalisation could reach N230 trillion by the end of 2026, roughly US$171 billion at the central bank’s 20 August rate. That requires the domestic savings pool to keep growing faster than it is being asked to fund.

The index is still up 54.3% for the year, so this is a correction inside a very strong run. What has changed is the composition of the buyers rather than the direction of prices.

There is also a supply story underneath the flows. Nigerian portfolios have been raising cash for a heavy pipeline of new listings, most conspicuously the Dangote refinery offering.

That is a healthy use of a domestic savings pool, and it is also a reason the secondary market has been leaking. Money committed to a primary issue has to come from somewhere.

Frequently Asked Questions

How much of Nigeria’s stock trading is domestic? Domestic investors accounted for N10.68 trillion, or 89.21%, of all transactions on the Nigerian Exchange in the first seven months of 2026. Foreign transactions were N1.29 trillion, or 10.79%. How far has the Nigerian market fallen? Between 10 and 20 August 2026 the All-Share Index fell 3.42% and market value dropped N5.44 trillion, about US$4.0 billion. The index is still up 54.3% for the year. Which stocks led the decline? Aradel Holdings fell 5.40% to N1,300.00 on 20 August, and the NGX Oil and Gas index lost 2.49%. UBA, Zenith and GTCO all closed lower. Are foreign investors leaving Nigeria? Foreign turnover is running below last year’s pace. N1.29 trillion over seven months annualises to about N2.21 trillion against N2.65 trillion in 2025, and the domestic share rose mainly because local volume nearly doubled.

World.title: D’Fab 4 brings The Beatles Show to Lamanai Riverside Retreat
World.content:
D’Fab 4 brings The Beatles Show to Lamanai Riverside Retreat

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): The Beatles are coming to Orange Walk, or as close as you can get.

D’Fab 4, a Beatles experience band, takes the stage live at Lamanai Riverside Retreat on Saturday, September 5 at 7pm.

The four piece delivers the songbook that defined a generation, from the early hits to the later work, played live by musicians who know the material inside out.



Opening the night is Bronnie.

Riverside Retreat provides the setting, right on the water, which makes for a very different concert night than a hall or a hotel ballroom.

Saturday, September 5. Doors and music from 7pm at Lamanai Riverside Retreat.
